meta.title: Riber SA: How CEO Annie Geoffroy Is Repositioning the World's Dominant Molecular Beam Epitaxy Equipment Maker—From Niche Compound-Semiconductor Tool Supplier to Silicon-Photonics Platform Company—While Expanding Margins, Growing Its Order Book Twenty-Four Percent, and Weathering Export-Control Headwinds in a Market Electrified by AI Infrastructure Build-Out
meta.abstract:
Riber SA (Euronext Growth Paris: ALRIB), headquartered in Bezons, France, is the world's leading supplier of molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) equipment—a class of ultra-high-vacuum semiconductor deposition reactors that produce the atomically precise compound-semiconductor layers required for 5G/6G radio-frequency transistors, VCSEL laser arrays, infrared detector focal planes, quantum-dot datacom lasers, and emerging photonic integrated circuits. Founded in 1964 and the only publicly listed pure-play MBE equipment company globally, Riber commands an installed base of more than 800 systems spanning six continents, giving it a durable aftermarket in effusion cells, spare parts, and service contracts that buffers the lumpy cadence of new-system revenues.

Under Chairwoman and CEO Annie Geoffroy, appointed in September 2023 and confirmed in a unified leadership role following the June 2024 governance restructuring, Riber has pursued three interlocking strategic priorities: (1) optimising profitability by improving gross margins and operating leverage, (2) deepening penetration of high-value production-system customers in Europe and North America as a counterweight to historically dominant Asian volumes, and (3) launching ROSIE (RIBER Oxide on Silicon Epitaxy)—a 300 mm-compatible, SEMI-standard-compliant oxide MBE platform that deposits barium titanate (BTO) on silicon substrates, enabling electro-optic modulators for AI data-centre interconnects and quantum-photonics applications.

The financial record under this strategy is notable: full-year 2024 net income rose 21% on 5% revenue growth to €41.2m; full-year 2025 net income rose 27% to €5.2m on revenues that declined 2% to €40.3m, with gross margins expanding from 36.1% to 38.6% and operating margins reaching 12.7%—demonstrating that earnings can compound while the top line absorbs macro volatility. The order book at 31 December 2025 stood at €26.9m (+24%), comprising six contracted MBE systems including four production machines and the first ROSIE platform, providing material 2026 revenue visibility.

The dossier examines three strategic narratives in depth: the ROSIE platform's potential to reposition Riber in the high-growth silicon-photonics equipment segment; the profitability inflection driven by production-system mix and aftermarket discipline; and the export-licence constraint that blocked an estimated €4m in 2025 revenues and represents the single most acute near-term risk to the 2026 growth outlook.

chapters.title: The Quiet Titan: Riber SA and the MBE Equipment Monopoly No One Talks About
chapters.body:
Somewhere inside an AI data-centre now under construction, a rack of optical transceivers will carry traffic at 800 gigabits per second across a wavelength that was impossible to generate reliably a decade ago. The semiconductor wafer at the heart of those transceivers was almost certainly grown in a machine built by a 119-person company in Bezons, France, trading on a small-cap exchange most institutional equity desks have never opened, and generating less than €50 million in annual revenues. That company is Riber SA. It is, by installed-base count, the world's dominant supplier of molecular beam epitaxy equipment — a position so structurally entrenched, and so widely ignored, that it constitutes one of the more unusual micro-cap anomalies in European industrial equities.

## A Monopoly Hiding in Plain Sight

MBE is not a niche curiosity. It is the deposition technique of last resort — the method that other semiconductor processes cannot replicate — for the atomically precise compound-semiconductor layers that enable 5G radio-frequency front ends, VCSEL arrays for facial recognition and automotive LiDAR, quantum-dot lasers for hyperscale optical interconnects, and infrared detector focal planes for military and space imaging. When device architects require layer thicknesses controlled to a single atomic monolayer, under ultra-high vacuum conditions below 10⁻¹⁰ torr, Riber's systems are on the short list; with more than 800 installations across six decades, they are overwhelmingly the incumbent choice.

Against that strategic position, the financial metrics are startling in their modesty. [Riber's 2025 results](https://www.riber.com/financial_documents/riber-delivers-strong-earnings-growth-in-2025/) show full-year revenues of €40.3 million — a 2.1% decline from 2024 — from just 12 machine deliveries, with an order book entering 2026 at €26.9 million, up 24% year-on-year. The company employs 119 people globally, maintains no financial debt, and trades on Euronext Growth Paris under the ticker ALRIB with thin float and negligible sell-side coverage. Yet net income in 2025 reached €5.2 million — a 27% year-on-year increase — at a 13.0% margin that most industrial equipment companies twice its size would envy.

## Three Threads, One Thesis

The analytical case for Riber resolves into three interlocking narratives that this dossier will examine in sequence. The first is market-relevance amplification: compound semiconductors have migrated from aerospace procurement cycles into the structural capital expenditure of connectivity infrastructure and AI compute, embedding Riber's installed base on the critical path of industries that are themselves in multi-decade expansion. The second is technology category creation: the ROSIE platform — Riber's fully automated, SEMI-compliant MBE system for depositing barium titanate on 300 mm silicon wafers — targets silicon photonics, a domain whose incumbent capital equipment suppliers have no oxide-MBE capability, offering Riber an addressable market that dwarfs its current revenue base. The third is a profitability inflection that has already begun: gross margins have expanded approximately 450 basis points since fiscal 2023, from roughly 34% to 38.6% in 2025, compressing operating costs against a broadly flat revenue line and producing a 53% cumulative increase in net income on a 3% cumulative revenue increase.

## The Numbers Behind the Narrative

| Metric | FY 2023 | FY 2024 | FY 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue (€m) | 39.2 | 41.2 | 40.3 |
| Gross margin | ~34% | 36.1% | 38.6% |
| Operating income (€m) | 4.5 | 4.5 | 5.1 |
| Net income (€m) | 3.4 | 4.1 | 5.2 |
| Net margin | 8.7% | 10.0% | 13.0% |

Chairwoman and CEO Annie Geoffroy, who assumed operational leadership in September 2023 and consolidated authority under a unified Board structure in June 2024, described 2025 as

> "an important milestone for RIBER, with a significant improvement in our profitability and the first commercial successes of our ROSIE platform."

The first two ROSIE orders — one from the Niels Bohr Institute's quantum-computing programme in Denmark, one from a US quantum-computing company in September 2025 — validate the platform's early commercial logic even before revenue scale is visible.

## The Risk Register

Honest accounting requires stating what the headline numbers obscure. H1 2025 revenues were €10.7 million, down 22% year-on-year, against an H2 of €29.5 million — a 73/27 back-half concentration driven by machine acceptance schedules that makes Riber genuinely difficult to own through the cycle. More structurally, export-licence refusals prevented the company from completing approximately €4 million of identified 2025 opportunities, and management's 2026 revenue growth guidance is explicitly conditioned on obtaining required licences. With Asia still representing 39.7% of 2025 revenues — down from 57.3% in 2024 but still substantial — geopolitical semiconductor equipment controls remain embedded in the financial outlook.

## Into 2026

The 2026 setup is more constructive than the muted 2025 revenue line suggests. In January 2026, Riber announced receipt of an MBE 6000 order from a Japanese customer for quantum-dot laser fabrication — the same 1,300 nm quantum-dot architecture now proliferating through AI data-centre transceiver supply chains. Simultaneously, ROSIE 2, a dual-chamber cluster version targeting higher wafer throughput for industrial customers, moved into manufacturing for 2026 delivery. Together, these developments position the current order book of €26.9 million as the floor rather than the ceiling of 2026 revenue visibility — provided the export-licence overhang clears. Whether Geoffroy's profitability discipline can convert that visibility into another year of margin expansion, and whether ROSIE's commercial seeding can grow from two units into a replicable revenue stream, is the question the subsequent chapters of this dossier will answer.

chapters.title: Vacuum, Epitaxy, and Sixty Years of Reinvention: The Corporate History of Riber SA
chapters.body:
## Origins in Ultra-High Vacuum, 1964

In 1964, four engineers whose names have not survived the public record established a small precision-engineering firm in Bezons, a river-bend suburb roughly twelve kilometres northwest of central Paris. The company they named Riber SA—an etymology no corporate filing or anniversary retrospective has ever formally explained—initially had little to do with semiconductor fabrication. Its early business was grounded in stainless-steel precision work: tungsten-inert-gas welding for ultra-high-vacuum hardware, and the European distribution of American-made ion pumps and micro-welders to the research laboratories then expanding rapidly across French universities and national institutes. The work was unglamorous but technically demanding, and it gave Riber's engineers an intimacy with extreme-vacuum engineering that would prove decisive in the decade to come.

The compound-semiconductor industry barely existed in 1964. Silicon was already the substrate of the integrated circuit, but gallium arsenide, indium phosphide, and the other III-V materials that would eventually power mobile communications and photonics were curiosities confined to a handful of physics departments. Riber, making flanges and distributing pumps, occupied a modest corner of the research infrastructure that would eventually give those materials a manufacturing pathway.

## The MBE Pivot, 1976–1978

The transformation began gradually in the mid-1970s, when Riber engineers started collaborating with academic pioneers to construct bespoke deposition systems for research groups studying compound-semiconductor thin films. Molecular beam epitaxy—MBE—is a physical vapour deposition technique executed under ultra-high-vacuum conditions below 10⁻¹⁰ torr, in which collimated beams of elemental or molecular species are directed at a heated crystalline substrate to grow atomically precise, single-crystal semiconductor layers. The method offered something that no prior deposition technique could reliably deliver: control down to a single atomic monolayer, with precise command over layer composition, thickness, and dopant profiles. For compound-semiconductor device researchers, it was a step-change in the same order of magnitude as the shift from vacuum tubes to transistors.

By 1976–1977, Riber's collaborative work had brought it into contact with a programme connected to Zhores Alferov of the Ioffe Institute in St. Petersburg—the physicist whose heterostructure research would eventually earn him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000. That connection proved catalytic. In 1978, Riber launched what it claims as the world's first turnkey MBE systems with guaranteed performance specifications: the MBE 500 and MBE 1000 Series. The distinction mattered commercially as well as technically. Prior MBE apparatus had been bespoke laboratory constructions; Riber was offering industrial customers a system with defined, warranted outcomes. The vacuum-hardware specialist had become, almost without intending to, the world's first commercial MBE equipment maker.

## Growth and Commitment, 1980–1994

The following decade and a half was marked by steady technical progress and a progressive deepening of market commitment. By 1984, Riber had reached the milestone of one hundred cumulative systems sold—a meaningful threshold in a market where each machine required months of design, fabrication, and commissioning, and where customers were research institutes and early compound-semiconductor fabs with long procurement cycles and high expectations.

The 1990 introduction of the MBE 49 marked a more significant technological advance: Riber's first fully automated industrial MBE prototype. Where earlier systems demanded constant manual intervention, the MBE 49 incorporated process automation that pointed toward the production-grade reliability the compound-semiconductor industry would eventually require. It was an engineering statement of intent—a proof that MBE could aspire to the throughput and repeatability of a manufacturing tool rather than a research instrument.

The most consequential strategic decision of this period came in 1994, when Riber's management chose to concentrate the company entirely on the MBE sector, divesting its residual vacuum hardware lines. This was not an obvious call. The compound-semiconductor equipment market remained small relative to the silicon tools business dominated by Applied Materials and Lam Research, and MBE—slower and more capital-intensive than competing deposition methods—was still regarded by some industry observers as a technique with permanently limited commercial scale. The 1994 focus decision rejected that view. Management judged that MBE's unmatched precision gave it an irreplaceable role wherever device performance demanded quantum-level control, and that a vertically concentrated pure-play could build application depth and customer relationships that a diversified equipment conglomerate would not prioritise. Thirty years of subsequent history validated the bet.

## Three Acquisitions, 2004–2015

Riber's growth from pure-play MBE tool maker to platform company was shaped materially by three targeted bolt-on acquisitions executed over an eleven-year span.

In 2004, the company acquired Addon, a French manufacturer of MBE effusion cells and associated components. The deal was strategically straightforward: effusion cells—the heated crucibles from which elemental beams are generated—wear out, need replacement, and must meet exacting specifications tied to the reactor design. Owning the component business deepened Riber's aftermarket revenue stream and tightened its relationship with the installed base, converting one-time system sales into recurring accessory and consumable revenue. The Addon acquisition effectively created the services and components segment that would eventually account for roughly a quarter of group revenues.

Four years later, in 2008, Riber moved into the United Kingdom with the acquisition of VG Semicon, a British MBE systems maker with its own reactor designs, an established European installed base, and longstanding relationships with UK compound-semiconductor research customers. VG Semicon brought complementary engineering IP and extended Riber's geographic reach at a moment when the European research market for III-V materials was expanding. The integration added customer relationships in British university and government laboratories that remain part of the installed base today.

The third acquisition, MBE Control Solutions in 2015, addressed a capability gap rather than a product or geography. The US firm provided software and automation capability for MBE process control, particularly relevant for the North American research market where university and corporate R&D customers demanded increasingly sophisticated recipe management and in-situ monitoring integration. Bringing that software competence in-house allowed Riber to deepen the technical differentiation of its systems and positioned the company for the more heavily automated production-platform designs that would follow.

## Governance and the Euronext Growth Listing

Riber has traded on Euronext Growth Paris under ticker ALRIB—ISIN FR0000075954—since its initial public offering, operating as one of the handful of French micro-cap industrial companies that have remained independently listed rather than being absorbed by larger equipment groups or taken private. For most of its public life, the company operated under a dual Management Board and Supervisory Board structure typical of certain French corporate forms, in which a multi-member operational board reported to a separate supervisory layer.

At the Combined General Meeting of 19 June 2024, shareholders voted to dissolve that structure and establish a single unified Board of Directors comprising seven members, aligned with the MiddleNext Corporate Governance Code for listed companies. The newly constituted board—including four independent directors alongside Annie Geoffroy as Chair and CEO, Pierre-Yves Kielwasser, and Bernard Raboutet—consolidated oversight and operational authority in a single governance layer. For a company of Riber's scale, the simplification was pragmatically sensible: dual-board structures impose administrative overhead that can constrain decision-making speed, and the MiddleNext framework's emphasis on independent director participation and transparent disclosure gave institutional credibility to a company that receives limited sell-side coverage.

## The Sixtieth Anniversary and the ROSIE Bet, 2024

In 2024, Riber reached its sixtieth year. The milestone offered the company's leadership an occasion to narrate, with some justification, a history characterised by disciplined reinvention rather than institutional inertia. From vacuum hardware distribution to MBE pioneer, from bespoke research tools to turnkey production systems, from single-product machine maker to integrated platform with components and software: each transition had followed a consistent logic of deepening technical capability and expanding the addressable market without abandoning the ultra-high-vacuum and epitaxial-growth expertise that had always been the company's core.

The launch of the ROSIE commercial programme—RIBER Oxide on Silicon Epitaxy—was announced against that backdrop. Where Riber's prior reinventions had remained within the III-V and II-VI compound-semiconductor domain, ROSIE carried the company's MBE expertise directly onto silicon, the substrate of the CMOS world. By depositing barium titanate and strontium titanate thin films on 300 mm silicon wafers in a SEMI-compliant, fully automated system designed to integrate with existing CMOS fab workflows, Riber was not abandoning sixty years of practice—it was extending that practice into an adjacent domain that silicon-photonics and quantum-computing customers could not access through any existing equipment supplier. The first two commercial ROSIE orders, received in 2025, confirmed that the pivot was more than engineering aspiration.

The pattern, surveyed across six decades, was consistent: find the boundary where ultra-high-vacuum precision can solve a problem that existing methods cannot, build the product, guarantee the performance, and remain. Bezons, 1964. Silicon photonics, 2024. The methodology had not changed.

chapters.title: Reactors, Sources, and ROSIE: The Product Architecture of the World's Leading MBE Equipment Supplier
chapters.body:
## The Physics of Atomically Abrupt

To understand why Riber SA exists—and why its systems command prices that exceed those of nearly every competing deposition technology—it is necessary to understand what molecular beam epitaxy actually does, and why nothing else does it the same way.

In a conventional chemical vapour deposition or atomic layer deposition reactor, precursor molecules arrive at the substrate surface already carrying chemical bonds that must be broken, leaving behind carbon, hydrogen, or chlorine contamination that perturbs the crystalline lattice. Sputtering offers high throughput but deposits amorphous or polycrystalline films with poorly controlled composition gradients. MBE is different in kind, not degree. Inside an MBE growth chamber, the operating pressure is maintained below 10⁻¹⁰ torr—lower than the atmospheric pressure on the surface of the Moon—ensuring that the mean free path of evaporated atoms exceeds the chamber diameter by orders of magnitude. Individual effusion cells, each a high-purity crucible heated to temperatures between roughly 200°C and 1,400°C depending on the element, emit collimated thermal beams of gallium, indium, aluminium, arsenic, phosphorus, or dopant species. These beams impinge on a single-crystal substrate—typically a GaAs, InP, GaN, or silicon wafer—maintained at a precisely controlled temperature and rotating at a few revolutions per minute to ensure compositional uniformity across the wafer surface. Because each arriving atom has insufficient energy to displace atoms already incorporated into the crystal, and because beam fluxes can be switched within fractions of a second using mechanical shutters, MBE can lay down semiconductor heterojunctions whose compositional transition occurs within a single atomic monolayer.

That capability is not merely an academic virtue. The quantum-well and quantum-dot device architectures that define modern telecommunications, 5G radio-frequency electronics, and increasingly AI data-centre interconnects depend on heterointerfaces that are atomically abrupt. A single layer of intermixing between GaAs and AlGaAs in a high-electron-mobility transistor (HEMT) structure degrades channel mobility and noise figure. Quantum-dot lasers emitting at 1,300 nm—the wavelength window preferred for silicon-photonic datacom transceivers—require InAs dot ensembles of controlled size and density embedded in an InGaAs matrix, a structure whose uniformity is directly tied to the precision of the deposition beam fluxes. Reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED), a diagnostic technique in which a low-energy electron beam is diffracted off the growing film surface and projected onto a fluorescent screen, provides real-time feedback on surface reconstruction and layer-by-layer growth mode that is simply unavailable in sealed CVD chambers. These structural requirements, combined with RHEED monitoring and in-situ reflectometry, make MBE not an exotic alternative but an irreplaceable process step for the device categories where it is deployed.

## MBE 6000: The Production Workhorse

Riber's flagship production system, the MBE 6000, has been the backbone of compound-semiconductor epiwafer foundry capacity since its introduction in 1998 and remains, nearly three decades later, the reference platform for high-volume automated MBE. The system accommodates multiple 3-inch, 4-inch, or 6-inch wafers loaded simultaneously via FOUP-compatible cassette automation—an interface standard originally developed for silicon CMOS fabs—allowing integration into cleanroom workflows that run twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. With thirteen source ports arrayed around the growth chamber, the MBE 6000 can host the full complement of group-III, group-V, dopant, and optional plasma sources required for complex multilayer device structures without breaking vacuum between material systems.

The system's headline operational specification—the ability to run continuously for more than ten months before requiring a scheduled maintenance vacuum break—is not a marketing claim but a commercial necessity for epiwafer producers whose customer delivery commitments are measured in volume per quarter. An unplanned vacuum break costs roughly three to five days of production time and several hundred kilogrammes of source replenishment; extending that interval directly translates to lower cost of ownership. GaAs-based HEMT and pseudomorphic HEMT (P-HEMT) wafers for 5G radio-frequency front ends, InP-based photonic device epiwafers, and quantum-dot 1,300 nm laser structures for datacom transceivers are among the device types the MBE 6000 produces in volume. Demand validation has arrived from multiple directions: in December 2023, an Asian epiwafer producer placed a dual-system order—two MBE 6000 units in a single transaction—and in January 2026 a Japanese customer ordered an additional unit specifically for quantum-dot laser fabrication serving the AI-infrastructure datacom supply chain.

## Research and Pilot Systems: The Installed-Base Engine

Below the MBE 6000 in the product hierarchy sits a family of single-wafer and cluster-tool configurations designed for research institutions, government laboratories, and corporate R&D centres. These systems are smaller in footprint, configurable for a single substrate or a handful of wafers per load, and engineered to accommodate a far wider range of material systems than production tools optimised for specific device families. Riber systems in this segment process III-V families including GaAs, InP, GaN, InAs, and InSb; II-VI families including CdTe, HgCdTe, and ZnSe for infrared detection applications; and nitride systems for wide-bandgap power electronics. The research-system procurement cycle is structurally different from production orders—driven by grant funding rounds, national laboratory capital budgets, and academic publishing ambitions rather than fab capacity expansions—but it generates an installed base whose growth compounds over decades.

Riber's global installation count now exceeds 800 systems. That number carries significance well beyond its face value. Each installed system is a recurring revenue attachment point for replacement effusion cells, source replenishment, process consumables, service contracts, and upgrade hardware; it also represents an institutional relationship with a materials scientist or process engineer who will, over a career spanning decades, write procurement specifications that cite Riber compatibility as a baseline requirement. The 800-system installed base constitutes, in effect, a platform standard for MBE research infrastructure.

## Sources, Cells, and Consumables: The Recurring Revenue Layer

MBE system hardware generates the headlines; MBE components and sources generate the cash-flow stability. Riber's components segment—contributing approximately €9.4 million, or 23.3% of 2025 total revenues—encompasses the full menu of consumable and wear items that the 800-system installed base requires throughout its operating life.

Effusion cells are the workhorse: resistive heating elements wound around high-purity pyrolytic boron nitride or alumina crucibles, available in standard and valved configurations that allow precise beam flux switching. Valved cracker sources for arsenic and phosphorus convert the elemental solid into the diatomic As₂ and P₂ species preferred for sharper heterointerface growth, while RF plasma sources ionise nitrogen or oxygen for nitride and oxide epitaxy applications. Substrate manipulators combine heaters, thermocouples, and rotational drives to maintain wafer temperature uniformity and growth-rate consistency. Cryogenic shrouds—liquid-nitrogen-cooled panels that surround the growth zone—act as cryopumps for background gas species, maintaining the ultra-high vacuum environment during prolonged deposition runs. All of these components wear, deplete, or require periodic replacement, creating a demand signal tied to the cumulative hours of operation across the installed base rather than to system sales in any given year.

In-situ characterisation tools occupy a premium tier within the components portfolio. EZ-CURVE measures real-time wafer curvature and strain during growth by tracking the deflection of a reflected laser beam across the wafer surface; strain accumulation during lattice-mismatched heteroepitaxy is a leading indicator of crystalline defect generation, and real-time curvature monitoring allows operators to adjust growth conditions before defect density compromises device performance. EZ-REF, Riber's in-situ reflectometry module, tracks the oscillating reflectance of the growing surface to measure layer thickness in real time during deposition, providing an independent check on growth rate without removing the wafer from vacuum. Together, these tools distinguish Riber's production systems from research-only competitors whose metrology is entirely ex-situ.

## ROSIE: Betting on the Silicon-Photonics Transition

The most consequential product development in Riber's recent history is a system that barely appears in the revenue figures yet may ultimately define the company's valuation trajectory. ROSIE—Riber Oxide on Silicon Epitaxy—is a fully automated MBE platform engineered specifically for the deposition of barium titanate (BTO) and strontium titanate (STO) thin films on 300 mm silicon wafers, designed from the ground up to integrate with the CMOS fabrication environment.

The scientific challenge ROSIE addresses is formidable. BTO, a perovskite ferroelectric with chemical formula BaTiO₃, exhibits a large Pockels electro-optic coefficient—the property whereby an applied electric field modulates the refractive index of the material—that makes it uniquely attractive for high-speed electro-optic modulators. Silicon itself has a negligibly small Pockels coefficient, which is why silicon-photonic modulators have historically relied on carrier-injection or carrier-depletion mechanisms with bandwidth and efficiency limitations. Integrating BTO on silicon would enable modulator bandwidths exceeding 100 Gbps with lower drive voltage and smaller footprint—a combination that data-centre hyperscalers and telecom equipment makers urgently want as AI infrastructure drives aggregate bandwidth requirements toward terabit-per-second scales.

The deposition challenge is that BTO is structurally incompatible with silicon. The lattice mismatch between BTO and Si is approximately 2%, and the transition from perovskite oxide to diamond-cubic semiconductor introduces ferroelectric domain boundaries and interfacial defects that degrade the electro-optic response if not controlled at the atomic level. MBE's ability to deposit the intermediate STO buffer layer atom by atom, at temperatures and pressures that suppress interdiffusion, is precisely what makes it the technique of choice—and what makes ROSIE defensible against CVD or PVD competitors who cannot replicate the interface quality.

ROSIE is built to 300 mm SEMI standards, with FOUP-to-FOUP cassette automation that allows the tool to accept wafer lots from and return them to standard silicon-fab material-handling systems without any manual transfer. That compatibility is not incidental; it is the entry ticket to a silicon-photonics fab environment where manual handling protocols are not acceptable. The POEM initiative—Photonic Oxide Epitaxy Modulator Technology—established with the Niels Bohr Institute's Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme (NQCP) in Denmark, serves as the pilot-line proving ground: ROSIE unit one was delivered to NQCP in the second half of 2025, and the POEM programme is scheduled to make BTO and STO thin-film samples on silicon available to the broader scientific and industrial community beginning in 2026, seeding the customer ecosystem Riber will need for subsequent commercial deployments.

> "2025 was an important milestone for RIBER, with a significant improvement in our profitability and the first commercial successes of our ROSIE platform," said Chairwoman and CEO Annie Geoffroy.

The second ROSIE order, placed by a US-based quantum-computing company in September 2025, extended ROSIE's geographic reach into North America within months of its commercial launch. ROSIE 2, a dual-chamber cluster version targeting higher wafer-per-hour throughput, is planned for manufacture in 2026—a configuration relevant to production-scale customers that require more than a few wafers per shift from a single deposition system.

## Roadmap and Market Positioning

The product-roadmap question is whether ROSIE can grow from a two-unit curiosity into a meaningful revenue contributor. Context is instructive. A production MBE 6000 system sells in a price range consistent with sophisticated compound-semiconductor capital equipment—broadly in the range of €2–4 million per unit, though Riber does not publish list prices. ROSIE, as a 300 mm SEMI-compliant tool with specialised oxide deposition capability targeting a nascent but well-capitalised customer segment, would plausibly command a premium relative to the MBE 6000—perhaps €5–8 million per unit—if comparisons to analogous silicon photonics capital equipment in the ALD or CVD space are instructive. Even at five units annually, ROSIE revenue could represent a material addition to a €40 million revenue base.

Beyond BTO, the oxide MBE platform that ROSIE establishes is extensible. Future variants could target strontium vanadate (SVO) for neuromorphic or correlated-oxide device research, vanadium dioxide (VO₂) for optical switching applications exploiting metal-insulator transitions, or lanthanum aluminate and related complex oxides for ferroelectric memories. The RHEED-equipped, in-situ-monitored architecture that underpins ROSIE transfers across these material systems without fundamental redesign. What Riber has built is not a single-material tool but an oxide-on-silicon platform—and the silicon-photonics market it is entering is one whose capital equipment has never before had a supplier with Riber's depth of UHV MBE expertise.

chapters.title: The Profitability Inflection: Revenue Trajectories, Margin Expansion, and Capital Structure at Riber SA
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Line That Flatlines, and Profits That Don't

The most important financial story at Riber SA is not the one the top-line revenue chart tells. Between fiscal year 2023 and fiscal year 2025, group revenues barely moved: €39.2 million, €41.2 million, €40.3 million—a three-year range of less than five percent. To a casual reader scanning a Bloomberg terminal, the company looks like a business in stasis. The income statement below the revenue line tells a different story entirely.

Net income over that same window grew from €3.4 million to €4.1 million to €5.2 million—a 53 percent cumulative increase on a 3 percent cumulative revenue increase. Operating income reached €5.1 million in fiscal 2025, equivalent to a 12.7 percent margin, up from 8.7 percent net margin just two years prior. Gross margin expanded by roughly 450 basis points across the cycle. This is not a revenue-growth story. It is a margin-engineering story, and understanding it requires reconstructing Riber's revenue base from its 2022 foundation.

[Riber SA investor relations](https://www.riber.com/finance/)

## From the 2023 Surge to Managed Stability

The fiscal year 2022 baseline, at approximately €27.8 million in implied revenues, understates the severity of the jump that followed. In fiscal 2023, Riber recorded €39.2 million in total revenues, a 41 percent increase that was almost entirely attributable to a single segment: MBE production systems. System sales were reported to have grown approximately 96 percent year-on-year, a near-doubling driven by the delivery and customer acceptance of a cohort of MBE 6000 production units to Asian compound-semiconductor foundries—principally in Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea—riding the capex wave of 5G radio-frequency front-end expansion.

The services and accessories segment, which had provided an above-average comparison base in 2022, fell approximately 21 percent in 2023 as one-time installation and commissioning revenues normalised. The divergence between segments was sharp and instructive: Riber was not diversifying its revenue mix in 2023; it was leveraging a single capital-equipment cycle.

The subsequent two years brought a different test. Fiscal 2024 revenues of €41.2 million (+4.9%) and fiscal 2025 revenues of €40.3 million (−2.1%) confirmed that the surge had been partially cyclical—but also revealed that management had used the breathing room to structurally reposition the cost base and product mix. [Semiconductor Today, April 2026](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news_items/2026/apr/riber-100426.shtml)

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (€m) | YoY Change | Gross Margin | Net Income (€m) | Net Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY 2022 | ~27.8 | — | ~n/d | — | — |
| FY 2023 | 39.2 | +41% | ~34% | 3.4 | 8.7% |
| FY 2024 | 41.2 | +4.9% | 36.1% | 4.1 | 10.0% |
| FY 2025 | 40.3 | −2.1% | 38.6% | 5.2 | 13.0% |

## The Anatomy of Margin Expansion

The 450-basis-point gross margin improvement from approximately 34 percent in fiscal 2023 to 38.6 percent in fiscal 2025 is not a rounding artefact. Three distinct forces drove it, and they reinforce each other.

The first is product-mix shift. In fiscal 2025, MBE systems generated approximately €30.9 million—76.7 percent of total revenues—from 12 machines delivered and accepted. Within that systems figure, the proportion attributable to production systems (the MBE 6000 and newer MBE 7000 platforms sold to epiwafer foundries) relative to smaller research-grade units carried meaningfully higher average selling prices. Production systems require extensive factory automation, multi-wafer cassette handling, and process qualification protocols that justify premium pricing; research units, sold in higher unit volume, carry narrower margins. As the revenue mix tilted toward production, blended gross margin lifted.

The second force is manufacturing overhead absorption. Riber's Bezons facility is a fixed-overhead operation: the engineering and technician workforce of roughly 119 staff, the UHV chamber fabrication infrastructure, and the application laboratory represent costs that do not scale linearly with revenue. As annual revenues stabilised above €40 million—roughly 45 percent above the pre-2023 base—the overhead absorption rate per shipped system improved without requiring incremental headcount. This is the operating leverage embedded in a low-volume, high-ASP equipment model.

The third force is accessories pricing discipline. The services and accessories segment—effusion cells, cracker sources, substrate manipulators, in-situ monitoring tools, and maintenance contracts—generated approximately €9.4 million in fiscal 2025 (23.3 percent of revenues). This segment declined 7.8 percent year-on-year in 2025, partly attributable to reduced procurement from US university laboratories facing federal budget constraints. Despite the volume headwind, management appears to have maintained or increased unit pricing on consumable components tied to the 800-unit worldwide installed base, protecting margin contribution even as volumes softened.

Operating income reached €5.1 million in 2025, a 12.7 percent operating margin, up 13.5 percent year-on-year. With tax and below-the-line items absorbing a narrow spread, net income of €5.2 million actually exceeded operating income in reported terms—yielding a 13.0 percent net margin, the highest in the company's recent history.

> "2025 represents an important milestone for RIBER, with a significant improvement in our profitability and the first commercial successes of our ROSIE platform." — Annie Geoffroy, Chairwoman and CEO [Riber SA press release, February 2026](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news_items/2026/feb/riber-030226.shtml)

## The Half-Year Problem: Structural Revenue Lumpiness

Any financial analysis of Riber that stops at annual figures risks fundamental misreading of the business. The intra-year revenue distribution is extreme and structurally driven.

In fiscal 2025, first-half revenues were €10.7 million—just 26.6 percent of the full-year total—while second-half revenues were €29.5 million, or 73.4 percent. H1 2025 was down 22 percent year-on-year; H2 2025 was up 7 percent. An investor reading only the interim report filed after H1 2025 would have encountered a business appearing to be in material decline. The full-year result was, in fact, a modest deterioration followed by a meaningful recovery.

This pattern is not accident or management misstep. MBE systems carry 12- to 18-month lead times from order to factory acceptance, and customer-acceptance milestones—the point at which revenue is formally recognised—are concentrated in the second half of Riber's fiscal year as machines are shipped, installed, qualified, and signed off. European production-system deliveries contributed materially to the H2 2025 recovery, as customers from within the region completed the acceptance process on units ordered in late 2024. [Riber SA investor relations](https://www.riber.com/financial_documents/2025-performance-driven-by-production-systems-and-the-rollout-of-rosie/)

The practical implication for investor communication is demanding: Riber must consistently pre-empt the interim-period optical distortion by disclosing order-book figures, unit-delivery timelines, and acceptance-stage status with enough granularity that analysts do not misread a lean H1 as a structural deterioration. With minimal sell-side coverage on Euronext Growth Paris, the risk of mispricing is elevated.

## Geography as Risk Indicator

The geographic revenue data in fiscal 2025 contains a dual signal. Asia's share fell from 57.3 percent of 2024 revenues to 39.7 percent in 2025; Europe's share rose from 35.7 percent to 45.1 percent; North America's share more than doubled from 7.1 percent to 15.2 percent.

On the surface, this looks like progress toward regional diversification—and on a structural horizon, it may be. But the immediate driver was simpler: European and North American customers completed acceptance on their machines in 2025, while several Asian opportunities were blocked. Riber disclosed that export-licence refusals prevented completion of approximately €4 million of commercial opportunities in 2025. Those foregone revenues almost certainly would have pushed Asian concentration higher and total revenues toward €44 million. The diversification in the 2025 geographic breakdown, in other words, is partly a residual of regulatory attrition rather than a deliberate reallocation of the customer base. Whether it proves durable depends on whether ROSIE and new research-system wins in Europe and North America can fill the gap as export controls on Asian customers remain in effect.

## A Balance Sheet Built for Resilience, Not Leverage

Riber's capital structure is deliberately conservative. Shareholders' equity stood at €27.3 million at 31 December 2025, up €3.7 million from the prior year, reflecting accumulated retained earnings from fiscal 2025 net income. Cash and cash equivalents were €7.5 million, down €1.1 million from €8.6 million at end-2024, with the reduction attributable to working-capital investment supporting H2 deliveries and the forthcoming dividend. The company carries no significant financial debt.

The return arithmetic on this structure is notable. Net income of €5.2 million on shareholders' equity of €27.3 million implies a return on equity of approximately 19 percent—competitive with many peer industrial equipment businesses carrying significantly more leverage. Riber achieves this without financial amplification.

Working capital dynamics are partially self-funding. Capital-equipment contracts of this scale typically carry advance payment provisions—customer deposits that effectively reduce the net working capital burden Riber faces ahead of delivery. The €7.5 million cash balance, while not a large absolute buffer, is adequate for a business whose major liability is the cost of building machines that are partly pre-funded by customer progress payments.

| Balance Sheet Item | FY 2025 (€m) | FY 2024 (€m) |
|---|---|---|
| Shareholders' Equity | 27.3 | 23.6 |
| Cash & Equivalents | 7.5 | 8.6 |
| Financial Debt | ~nil | ~nil |
| Return on Equity (implied) | ~19% | ~17% |

## The Order Book as Forward Compass

Because Riber's revenue recognition is acceptance-milestone-driven, the order book is the primary forward-revenue indicator available to investors. At 31 December 2025, the backlog stood at €26.9 million, up 24 percent from €21.7 million a year earlier. [GlobeNewswire, April 2025](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/04/09/3058110/0/en/RIBER-reports-solid-growth-in-sales-and-earnings-in-2024.html)

The composition matters. Systems backlog of €20.3 million covered six contracted units: four production-system orders (MBE 6000/7000 variants), one ROSIE platform unit, and one other system. Services and accessories backlog of €6.6 million was up 31 percent year-on-year, an encouraging signal for the recurring revenue base. Applying a standard 12- to 18-month delivery-to-acceptance timeline, the systems backlog entering 2026 provides near-complete coverage of expected 2026 system revenue under a base-case scenario—before accounting for any new orders booked during the fiscal year. The January 2026 MBE 6000 order from a Japanese quantum-dot laser customer, announced after the balance-sheet date, added to that pipeline.

## The Dividend: A Signal, Not a Strain

The Board's proposal of a €0.10 per share dividend for fiscal 2025—payable June 24, 2026, a 25 percent increase over the €0.08 per share paid for fiscal 2024—communicates confidence without straining the balance sheet. With approximately 21.25 million shares outstanding, the total dividend payment approximates €2.1 million, representing a payout ratio of roughly 40 percent of the €5.2 million net income.

This is a sustainable posture. The progressive policy—two consecutive increases, from a nominal base—signals management's conviction that the profitability improvement is structural rather than cyclical. A 40 percent payout retains €3.1 million annually for internal reinvestment: ROSIE 2 manufacturing, R&D on BTO-on-silicon process development, and the working-capital requirements of a growing order book. The dividend yield, against the share price that prevailed after the stock's reported re-rating through early 2026, is modest in absolute terms but functionally irrelevant to the investment case—what matters is the signal of earnings durability it encodes.

The financial picture that emerges from this reconstruction is of a company that managed a one-time revenue surge in 2023 with discipline, held revenues broadly flat across 2024–2025 while expanding margins by nearly five gross-margin percentage points, and entered 2026 with its largest order book in recent history. The top line may not yet reflect the ROSIE opportunity or the full normalisation of Asian export flows. But the income statement already reflects a business that has learned—under Geoffroy's stewardship—to extract more value from each euro of revenue it books.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Re-Rating Problem

Any attempt to value Riber SA with precision must begin with an honest acknowledgment of its market structure. Trading on Euronext Growth Paris under the ticker ALRIB.PA with a float of approximately 21.25 million shares and minimal sell-side coverage, the stock's price discovery mechanism is thin enough that published market-capitalisation figures diverged across data sources by a factor of nearly three as of the frozen snapshot date. Working from the reported share count and a recent price range, market capitalisation as of late May 2026 fell within an approximate band of €115 million to €320 million ($124 million to $346 million), with the upper end consistent with the extraordinary 365-day price appreciation of roughly 384 percent that Riber's shares had registered through the snapshot window. At 21.25 million shares outstanding, a price near €15 per share—implying a market cap of roughly €319 million—aligns with the upper boundary and with commentary suggesting a dramatic ROSIE-driven re-rating. All multiples below are presented against both the lower and upper bounds of this range; investors should treat the midpoint as a working estimate, not a firm figure.

## Current Multiples: Expensive by History, Defensible by Trajectory

Against fiscal 2025 net income of €5.2 million ($5.6 million) and operating income of €5.1 million, the implied trailing price-to-earnings multiple at the midpoint market cap of approximately €215 million was roughly 41 times—elevated for a manufacturer of industrial equipment, modest by the standards of capital-equipment companies successfully commercialising platform technologies. At the lower bound of €115 million the trailing P/E compressed to approximately 22 times, which would represent fair value for a steady-state niche equipment business growing profits at mid-single-digit rates. At the upper bound of €320 million the multiple expanded to roughly 62 times—territory typically reserved for software or high-growth semiconductor equipment franchises with demonstrated long-cycle revenue expansion.

Enterprise value, adjusted for the debt-free balance sheet and €7.5 million in year-end 2025 cash, ranged from approximately €107 million to €313 million. Against estimated EBITDA in the neighborhood of €6.5 million to €7.0 million (operating income of €5.1 million plus estimated depreciation and amortisation for a 119-person manufacturer), the EV/EBITDA range ran from roughly 15 times at the low end to 45 times at the high end. EV/Revenue, applied to fiscal 2025's €40.3 million ($43.5 million) in sales, ranged from 2.7 times to 7.8 times. Price-to-book, using shareholders' equity of €27.3 million, ranged from 4.2 times to 11.7 times—the upper end extraordinary for a capital-equipment manufacturer without an embedded software margin structure.

Historically, before the 2025–2026 re-rating, Riber traded at trailing P/E multiples in the 12-to-20 times range during periods of ordinary profitability. The ROSIE commercialisation announcements and the sustained margin expansion documented across 2023–2025 appear to have compressed the discount investors previously assigned for revenue lumpiness and export-concentration risk, lifting the implied multiple well above that historical band. The re-rating, in other words, has already happened; the valuation debate is whether it was justified and whether there is further upside.

## Peer-Group Comparison

Constructing a peer group for Riber is inherently imprecise. No publicly listed company operates as a pure-play MBE equipment supplier at comparable scale; DCA Instruments and SVT Associates are private. The closest listed analogue is [Veeco Instruments](https://www.veeco.com/) (Nasdaq: VECO), which competes in compound-semiconductor deposition with its MOCVD and ion-beam systems and serves many of the same end markets, though at roughly fifteen times Riber's revenue. The table below assembles a peer set of specialty semiconductor capital-equipment companies, acknowledging that size and product-scope mismatches make direct multiple comparisons illustrative rather than conclusive.

| Company | Ticker | FY Rev (approx.) | Trailing P/E | EV/EBITDA | EV/Rev | Gross Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Riber SA** (mid-cap est.) | ALRIB.PA | €40M ($43M) | ~41x | ~30x | ~5x | 38.6% |
| **Riber SA** (low-cap est.) | ALRIB.PA | €40M ($43M) | ~22x | ~16x | ~2.7x | 38.6% |
| Veeco Instruments | VECO | ~$600M | ~18x | ~12x | ~2.0x | ~46% |
| Onto Innovation | ONTO | ~$1.0B | ~22x | ~14x | ~3.5x | ~52% |
| Photronics | PLAB | ~$900M | ~12x | ~8x | ~1.5x | ~38% |
| Camtek | CAMT | ~$400M | ~28x | ~18x | ~4.0x | ~52% |
| Cohu | COHU | ~$500M | ~20x | ~11x | ~1.5x | ~47% |

The table underscores the valuation tension at the upper bound. Riber's midpoint EV/Revenue and EV/EBITDA multiples exceeded those of Onto Innovation and Camtek—both faster-growing, better-capitalised businesses with diversified product portfolios and established institutional followings. The premium is only defensible if ROSIE is assigned material option value and if margin expansion continues. At the lower-bound market cap, Riber's multiples are broadly in line with Photronics and Cohu—appropriate for a profitable niche equipment business with a strong installed base but without a demonstrated platform-growth catalyst.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Current Price Implies

A simplified discounted-cash-flow framing helps anchor the debate. Assume fiscal 2025 free cash flow approximated net income minus working-capital investment—call it €4.0 to €4.5 million, given the cash balance declined €1.1 million year-on-year despite strong earnings, reflecting working-capital build for H2 deliveries. Discounting a steady-state free-cash-flow stream of €4.5 million at a 10 percent cost of equity (appropriate for a single-country-listed, thinly traded micro-cap with export-licence risk) and applying a 3 percent terminal growth rate yields an intrinsic value of approximately €105 million—call it €5 per share. The market at the upper bound was pricing in something far more optimistic: to justify €320 million, the implied free-cash-flow trajectory required either a sustained multi-year expansion of margins toward 18–20 percent and/or a ROSIE revenue ramp delivering €15–25 million in incremental system revenue by 2028–2029. That is achievable but speculative.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case** — price implication: €18–22 per share (~€380–470 million market cap). ROSIE secures four to six orders annually beginning in 2026, with unit ASPs in the €8–10 million range typical of 300 mm CMOS-compatible tools. Total revenue approaches €60–65 million by fiscal 2027. Net margins, already at 13 percent and rising, reach 17–18 percent through operating leverage on the fixed cost base. The market assigns a 40–45 times forward P/E to a company demonstrating a credible silicon-photonics platform franchise—a multiple consistent with high-growth specialty equipment names. Export-licence issues normalise or are routed around through European and North American customer diversification.

**Base case** — price implication: €10–14 per share (~€210–300 million market cap). ROSIE contributes two to three systems per year through 2027, adding €16–24 million in incremental revenue above the MBE baseline. Total revenue reaches €50–55 million by fiscal 2027. Net margins hold in the 14–15 percent range. The market assigns a 30–35 times forward P/E, reflecting a growth-oriented equipment business with meaningful platform optionality but unproven at scale. Export-licence headwinds persist but are manageable, with €3–5 million of annual revenue at risk.

**Bear case** — price implication: €3–5 per share (~€65–105 million market cap). Export-licence refusals intensify in 2026, blocking €6–8 million of the backlog and forcing revenue back toward €35–37 million. ROSIE adoption stalls at two units and the Niels Bohr/NQCP pilot line fails to catalyse replicable commercial orders. Net income reverts toward €3.5–4.0 million. With no evidence of platform scale, the market de-rates Riber back toward historical norms of 18–22 times trailing earnings, consistent with a well-run but cyclical niche equipment supplier.

## What the Market Was Pricing In

By the snapshot date, the weight of the evidence suggested the market had adopted something close to the base-to-bull transition scenario—pricing in continued profitability improvement, modest ROSIE traction, and an order-book conversion cadence supported by the €26.9 million backlog entering 2026. The 384-percent price appreciation over the prior twelve months implied that this re-rating was largely already embedded in the share price, leaving the risk-reward asymmetric for new buyers: the bull case required ROSIE to perform as a genuine platform product in a market—silicon photonics fab tooling—that had never before been addressed by MBE equipment, while the bear case required only that the status quo deteriorate modestly.

The gap between consensus (essentially non-existent, given negligible sell-side coverage) and the dossier's read was less about direction than about timing. A company growing net income at 27 percent annually on a stable revenue base, with no debt, a 24-percent increase in its order book, and a demonstrated ability to secure payments from institutions at the technology frontier of quantum-computing hardware deserved a re-rating. Whether the market anticipated that re-rating by twelve to eighteen months too early—or priced it precisely—depended on variables that only fiscal 2026 revenue conversion could answer.

chapters.title: Cadence and Commentary: Reading Riber's Quarterly Earnings Through the Cycle
chapters.body:
## A Three-Year Profit Arc in a Revenue-Flat Business

The fiscal 2023 results announcement gave investors their first clear signal that Riber SA's financial character had changed. Revenue that year reached [€39.2 million](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news_items/2025/feb/riber-030225.shtml), a 41% jump from fiscal 2022's €27.8 million driven almost entirely by a near-doubling in MBE systems deliveries, and net income landed at €3.4 million—an 8.7% margin. For a company that had spent years generating thin or inconsistent returns from its position as the world's leading molecular beam epitaxy equipment maker, the numbers marked a baseline shift. Revenue scale had arrived. The open question was whether management could translate volume into durable margin.

Over the following twenty-four months, the answer came in increments. Fiscal 2024 delivered [revenues of €41.2 million, a 4.9% increase](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/04/09/3058110/0/en/RIBER-reports-solid-growth-in-sales-and-earnings-in-2024.html), alongside net income of €4.1 million, up 21% year-on-year—more than four times the rate of top-line growth. Operating income reached €4.5 million, a 14.4% improvement, with income from ordinary operations representing 11% of revenue. Gross margin expanded from approximately 34% in fiscal 2023 to 36.1% in 2024, reflecting a deliberate mix shift toward higher-ASP production systems and tighter discipline in the accessories segment. For the first time in recent memory, Riber was demonstrating the operating leverage latent in a business where fixed costs—its Bezons engineering workforce, its UHV manufacturing infrastructure—could be spread across a larger and better-priced revenue base.

## The 2024 Results and a Carefully Hedged 2025 Posture

The April 2025 full-year 2024 results communication contained one notable act of guidance conservatism. Management explicitly reserved its position on fiscal 2025 revenue guidance, citing what the company described as the uncertainties linked to the application of US customs duties and the economic environment. The language was deliberate. Riber was signalling to investors that the macro backdrop—specifically the tariff environment that was beginning to complicate semiconductor equipment supply chains in the first half of 2025—introduced enough demand-timing uncertainty that no forward revenue commitment would be responsible.

In hindsight, that caution was both validated and somewhat overdone. [Full-year 2025 revenues came in at €40.3 million](https://www.riber.com/financial_documents/riber-delivers-strong-earnings-growth-in-2025/), a 2.1% decline from the 2024 peak, meaning the absolute revenue impact of the headwinds management had flagged was real but limited in scale. What management did not hedge was the profitability trajectory. Net income rose 27.1% to €5.2 million—a 13.0% margin—as gross margin expanded a further 250 basis points to 38.6% and operating income grew 13.5% to €5.1 million, reaching 12.7% of revenue. The 2024 guidance posture, then, was not pessimism but precision: management accurately identified the revenue risk while simultaneously delivering the sharpest earnings growth in its recent history by maintaining operational discipline under pressure. The episode is instructive about how Geoffroy's leadership handles investor communications—conservative on revenue, confident on the margin trajectory it can control.

## H1 Weakness and the Structural Logic of Back-Half Concentration

The first-half 2025 earnings release tested investor patience. [H1 2025 revenues of €10.7 million represented a 22% year-on-year decline](https://www.riber.com/financial_documents/2025-performance-driven-by-production-systems-and-the-rollout-of-rosie/) and just 26.6% of full-year revenue, compressing profitability sharply relative to prior-year comparisons. For an investor unfamiliar with MBE equipment delivery mechanics, the interim numbers might have signalled a demand shortfall.

Management's communication was consistent with prior guidance framing: MBE system revenue is structurally back-half weighted because delivery schedules are governed by customer factory readiness, wafer-acceptance testing protocols, and the multi-month lead times embedded in production-system builds. H2 2025 delivered €29.5 million, up 7% year-on-year, confirming that the H1 softness was timing, not volume destruction. The 73%/27% H2/H1 revenue split is not aberrant; it is the structural cadence of a business where a single machine delivery can be worth several million euros and a one-quarter slip in customer site preparation materially redistributes the annual revenue profile. Riber did not issue interim guidance revisions during the weak first half, and by retaining its medium-term objectives language through the period, management signalled confidence in the H2 recovery without making explicit quantitative commitments it would have had difficulty defending if execution had slipped.

## Services: Dip, Then Indicated Recovery

| Segment | FY 2024 | FY 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| MBE Systems | ~€31.8m | €30.9m | −2.8% |
| Services & Accessories | ~€9.4m | €9.4m (est.) | −7.8% |
| **Total** | **€41.2m** | **€40.3m** | **−2.1%** |

The services and accessories segment—effusion cells, cryogenic sources, substrate manipulators, maintenance contracts—generated [approximately €9.4 million in fiscal 2025](https://www.riber.com/financial_documents/2025-performance-driven-by-production-systems-and-the-rollout-of-rosie/), a 7.8% decline from the prior year. Management attributed the shortfall primarily to US government budgetary constraints that constrained university laboratory procurement, particularly in the North American research market served by the Riber Inc. subsidiary. The mechanism is straightforward: when US federal research budgets tighten at the agency level—affecting grants that flow to university MBE laboratories—discretionary spending on replacement sources, components, and service renewals is deferred.

What the 2025 income statement decline obscures is the forward signal embedded in the order book. Services backlog entering 2026 grew 31% year-on-year, implying a recovery in service-contract renewals, component orders, and maintenance engagements that was beginning to fill the pipeline even as the revenue year was closing. The divergence between the in-year revenue decline and the end-of-year backlog growth reflects both the lumpy timing of service contract renewals and a probable bottoming in university procurement constraints as US federal budgets stabilised.

## The Export-Licence Disclosure

No Riber earnings communication in 2025 could be fully assessed without engaging with the export-licence topic. Management disclosed that refusals of export licence applications blocked approximately [€4 million of identified commercial opportunities](https://www.riber.com/financial_documents/riber-delivers-strong-earnings-growth-in-2025/) in 2025. Against a full-year revenue base of €40.3 million, that represents roughly 10% of delivered revenue—a material quantum by any measure, and a direct consequence of semiconductor equipment trade controls tightening around Asia-Pacific markets, particularly China-adjacent customers.

The framing for 2026 was explicit about the conditionality. Riber stated its revenue-growth outlook was *subject to obtaining the export licences required to materialise the identified opportunities*. That language places a structural qualifier on any bullish 2026 revenue forecast: the upside case is real and order-book supported, but its realisation depends on a regulatory variable Riber does not control. Geographically, Asia accounted for 57.3% of 2024 revenue before falling to 39.7% in 2025 as European and North American deliveries accelerated—a mix shift that partially insulated the full-year outturn but which also reveals that the company's most commercially active growth region remains exposed to licence risk.

## Reading the 2026 Setup

The order book entering fiscal 2026 stood at [€26.9 million, a 24% increase](https://www.riber.com/financial_documents/2025-performance-driven-by-production-systems-and-the-rollout-of-rosie/) over the prior year-end, comprising six contracted systems and a €6.6 million services backlog. In January 2026, Riber announced an MBE 6000 production-system order from a Japanese customer for quantum-dot laser fabrication targeting the datacom sector—a direct signal that demand for 1,300 nm lasers in AI-infrastructure optical transceivers was converting into capital equipment orders. Two European MBE 6000 production-system orders were announced in December 2025, reinforcing the geographic diversification that partially hedged the export-licence risk embedded in the Asian pipeline.

Against this backdrop, Geoffroy's communications framed 2025 not as an endpoint but as an inflection:

> 2025 marks an important milestone for Riber, with a significant improvement in our profitability and the first commercial successes of our ROSIE platform.

And on continuity of direction:

> RIBER remains committed to its medium-term objectives.

The cumulative earnings arc from 2023 to 2025 tells a coherent story: revenue essentially flat across a three-year period, but net income compounding at 24% per year, gross margin expanding 450 basis points, and operating income nearly doubling from an estimated sub-€2.5 million level in 2022 to €5.1 million in 2025. The business Geoffroy inherited was commercially capable but financially under-leveraged. The business entering 2026—with a record-forward order book, a nascent ROSIE revenue stream, and three consecutive years of margin expansion—is structurally different, even if the revenue headline does not yet reflect it.

| Metric | FY 2023 | FY 2024 | FY 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | €39.2m | €41.2m | €40.3m |
| Revenue Growth | +41% | +4.9% | −2.1% |
| Gross Margin | ~34% | 36.1% | 38.6% |
| Operating Income | — | €4.5m (11.0%) | €5.1m (12.7%) |
| Net Income | €3.4m | €4.1m | €5.2m |
| Net Margin | 8.7% | 10.0% | 13.0% |
| Net Income Growth | — | +21% | +27% |

The numbers compress a management thesis into a table: revenue stability is not stagnation when the margin conversion is this consistent. Whether 2026 adds the revenue growth dimension to complete the re-rating narrative depends, in no small part, on decisions made in French export-control offices rather than in Bezons.

chapters.title: Annie Geoffroy and the Board: Leadership Structure, Director Profiles, and Governance at a Micro-Cap MBE Pioneer
chapters.body:
## Annie Geoffroy: The Transition Manager Who Stayed

When Annie Geoffroy stepped down from her role as President of Riber's Supervisory Board in September 2023 and accepted appointment as President of the Management Board, the move carried the unmistakable signature of a governance system under pressure. Transition managers — professionals hired to stabilise and redirect organisations at inflection points rather than to build multi-year legacies — do not typically migrate from the oversight tier to the executive tier of the same company. That Geoffroy did so, and that shareholders ratified the arrangement, said something pointed about the state of Riber's leadership bench at the time and about the board's confidence in her ability to carry the company through what would prove to be one of its more consequential strategic pivots.

Geoffroy, approximately 70 years old at the time of writing, trained at ESCP Europe — one of the French grandes écoles de commerce whose graduates populate the upper ranks of Paris-listed industrial companies — and holds a DESS (Diplôme d'Études Supérieures Spécialisées) in Management Control, a credential oriented toward financial oversight and operational restructuring rather than pure general management. Her career followed those contours: a succession of roles in French industrial companies where she applied financial discipline and operational transformation, culminating in a formalised transition-management practice she established in 2015. [Source: La Bourse et la Vie](https://www.labourseetlavie.com/strategie-et-resultats/annie-geoffroy-presidente-directrice-generale-riber-nous-avons-vocation-a-elargir-notre-marche) Her entry into the Riber ecosystem was through the supervisory function — a natural landing point for a governance-oriented professional — where she oversaw the three-member Management Board that included Michel Picault and Emmanuel Routier.

The September 2023 inversion of her role, from watcher to operator, has not been publicly explained with precision. No departure of a prior CEO has been announced in investor relations materials reviewed through the frozen window of 23 May 2026, and neither Riber's annual accounts nor its AGM documentation identifies a specific triggering event. What is visible is the outcome: executive authority consolidated in Geoffroy's hands nine months before the formal governance restructuring that would enshrine that consolidation permanently.

## The June 2024 Restructuring: From Dual Board to Unified Governance

The Combined General Meeting of 19 June 2024 was the formal ratification of a direction already established in practice. [Source: Marketscreener](https://www.marketscreener.com/quote/stock/RIBER-4786/news/RIBER-Report-on-the-Combined-General-Meeting-from-June-19-2024-47003335/) Shareholders voted to dissolve Riber's dual-structure governance — the Management Board responsible for day-to-day execution, the Supervisory Board responsible for oversight — and replace it with a single unified Board of Directors, a format more typical of French small-caps and expressly contemplated under the MiddleNext Corporate Governance Code to which Riber aligns.

The rationale for the conversion, as articulated in Riber's investor communications, was simplification and decisional efficiency. The dual structure, inherited from an earlier era of French corporate law, imposed a layer of procedural friction between strategic intent and operational execution that was arguably unnecessary for a company of 119 employees and sub-€50 million in revenues. For a micro-cap with a CEO who already wore the Management Board President hat, the Supervisory Board had become a constitutional formality. Eliminating it collapsed the governance architecture to a single board of seven directors — five of whom are classified as independent under MiddleNext criteria — with a three-year mandate running through the 2027 AGM deliberating on FY 2026 accounts.

The newly constituted board unanimously appointed Geoffroy Chairwoman and Chief Executive Officer, combining both titles in a single person for the first time in the company's history. Under the MiddleNext Code, the combination of Chair and CEO roles is permissible for smaller listed issuers, though the code recommends the designation of a lead independent director as a structural counterweight. Whether Riber has formally identified a senior independent director from within the five independent members of the board — a disclosure that would typically appear in the annual reference document — had not been confirmed in investor relations materials reviewed through the frozen window.

## The Board: Seven Directors, Five Independent

The seven-member board assembled at the June 2024 general meeting covers a range of professional backgrounds, though detailed public biographies remain fragmentary for several members.

**Sylviane Troadec** holds an independent classification and represents a governance-oriented profile consistent with the audit and oversight functions her presence likely serves.

**Nicolas Grandjean** carries the most intellectually specific signal of any board appointment. A French academic named Nicolas Grandjean is among Europe's most cited researchers in III-V nitride semiconductor physics, affiliated with EPFL's Institute of Physics in Lausanne where his group works on GaN and InGaN heterostructures — precisely the material systems grown by Riber's industrial MBE platforms. If, as the available record suggests, the Grandjean on the Riber board is the EPFL researcher, his presence as an independent director is unusual and deliberate: it embeds deep compound-semiconductor expertise at the governance level, creates a channel between Riber's product roadmap and the European academic MBE community, and signals to prospective customers in university and research segments that Riber's board is technically credible rather than purely commercially oriented. A potential complexity — the academic community's role as both customer and oversight body — merits periodic review, though for a company of Riber's scale the arrangement is common practice.

**Didier Cornardeau** and **Alexandre Jevakhoff** both carry independent classifications. Jevakhoff's name appears in French industrial and financial circles, suggesting a background in industrial or financial management, though detailed biographical disclosure in Riber's public materials is limited.

**Pierre-Yves Kielwasser** and **Bernard Raboutet** do not carry independent classifications in the June 2024 board composition, placing them in the two non-independent seats alongside Geoffroy's combined Chair/CEO role. Their specific professional connections to Riber — whether through prior shareholding, commercial relationships, or legacy management ties — are not detailed in available investor relations materials.

The five-of-seven independent director ratio exceeds the one-third independence floor recommended for smaller issuers under MiddleNext, a proportionally strong result for a micro-cap whose governance infrastructure remains relatively lean.

## The Invisible CFO and the Operational Layer

Riber's investor relations materials present Geoffroy as the singular public face of management. No Chief Financial Officer is identified separately in investor communications, earnings releases, or governance disclosures reviewed through the frozen window. The company's financial accounts are signed at the management level without naming a distinct CFO responsible for investor and creditor relations in the conventional sense.

Michel Picault and Emmanuel Routier, both of whom served as members of the prior Management Board alongside Geoffroy, are not identified in public materials as having retained executive titles — CFO, COO, or equivalent — following the June 2024 restructuring. Whether either retains an operational or divisional management role internal to the organisation is not determinable from public disclosures. The silence is not unusual for a French small-cap of this scale; management disclosure requirements under Euronext Growth are lighter than those applicable to Euronext's regulated market, and it is common for functional executives below the CEO level to remain effectively invisible to external observers.

The practical consequence is that investors and analysts interface with Riber almost entirely through Geoffroy herself — a concentration of communication authority that mirrors the concentration of governance authority and creates a dependency worth monitoring.

## Auditors: A French Statutory Peculiarity

The appointment of both KPMG and RSM Paris as co-statutory auditors (Commissaires aux comptes) is not unusual in the French listed-company context; French company law has historically required two independent Commissaires aux comptes for companies above certain thresholds, a dual-audit structure with no direct equivalent in Anglo-Saxon governance frameworks. The arrangement is designed to provide a check on the single-auditor concentration risk common in US and UK practice — each firm independently certifies the accounts, with discrepancies between them theoretically surfacing reporting conflicts. For Riber, the pairing of a global Big Four firm (KPMG) with a mid-tier specialist (RSM Paris) likely reflects the historical evolution of auditor relationships rather than a deliberate choice architecture; no audit qualifications, emphasis-of-matter paragraphs, or material restatements have been noted in accounts reviewed through the frozen window.

## Succession Planning: The Unaddressed Question

The most consequential governance gap at Riber, given the leadership structure described above, is succession planning. Geoffroy is approximately 70 years old, arrived with an explicit transition-manager mandate, and has in less than three years executed a profitability inflection, launched ROSIE commercially, and repositioned the board structure. She has not publicly indicated a tenure horizon.

Riber's disclosure on succession planning, to the extent it exists in investor materials reviewed through the frozen window, is minimal. The MiddleNext Code recommends that boards address succession for executive leadership as part of their annual governance review; whether the board has a concrete internal candidate, a defined external search protocol, or merely a passive acknowledgement of the issue is not determinable from public records.

The stakes of an unplanned transition are material. ROSIE's commercial success depends not only on technology execution but on Geoffroy's ability to navigate export-licence applications with French and European regulatory authorities — a relationship-intensive activity where individual leadership continuity matters. The POEM partnership with NQCP, the second ROSIE order with the unnamed US quantum-computing company, and the emerging BTO/STO sample seeding programme for the 2026 customer ecosystem all represent threads whose continuity would require deliberate institutional knowledge transfer. A board that has concentrated authority so tightly in one person carries an obligation to address what happens when that person departs; at the time of the frozen window, that obligation appeared unmet.

chapters.title: Universities, Foundries, and Quantum Labs: Riber's Global Customer Base Across Six End Markets
chapters.body:
## The Production Anchor: Compound-Semiconductor Foundries

Riber's commercial gravity begins where semiconductor manufacturing does: in the epiwafer foundry. Compound-semiconductor producers—the firms that grow III-V layers on substrate wafers and sell them to device integrators—represent the single largest demand node for Riber's MBE 6000 and MBE 7000 production systems, machines priced broadly in the €3–10m range and designed for uninterrupted multi-wafer throughput over production cycles spanning months.

The most prominently named of these customers is [IQE plc](https://www.iqep.com), listed on London's AIM market, which supplies GaAs and InP epiwafers for VCSELs embedded in Apple's Face ID facial-recognition arrays, as well as HEMT wafers for 5G radio-frequency front ends and multi-junction photovoltaic cells for concentrator solar.
