IQE's capex cycle functions as a leading indicator for Riber's order book: when IQE expands capacity—as it did aggressively in the 2019–2021 VCSEL super-cycle—Riber benefits directly; when IQE tightens capital expenditure in response to inventory corrections or customer demand softness, the transmission into Riber's systems pipeline is correspondingly rapid. Coherent Corp (formerly II-VI Incorporated), the US-based vertically integrated photonics conglomerate, represents a second named relationship in the production-systems tier. Beyond these flagship names, a constellation of unnamed Asian epiwafer producers in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and China has historically constituted Riber's deepest production-system demand base.

That Asian concentration carried a structural cost that became visible in 2025. Asia accounted for 57.3% of Riber's revenue in fiscal 2024; by fiscal 2025 that share had contracted to 39.7% — a reduction of nearly eighteen percentage points in a single year. The proximate cause was not demand destruction but regulatory friction: Riber disclosed that export-licence refusals blocked approximately €4 million of identified commercial opportunities during 2025, a figure material against annual revenues of €40.3 million. The company's 2026 guidance for revenue growth is explicitly conditional on obtaining required export authorisations, underscoring that trade controls on semiconductor capital equipment are not a transient event but a persistent structural constraint embedded in the Asian customer segment.

## The European Surge: Structural Diversification or Timing Artifact?

Against the Asian retreat, Europe expanded from 35.7% of revenue in 2024 to 45.1% in 2025, and North America from 7.1% to 15.2%. The question worth posing is whether this reflects durable diversification or the timing of specific large deliveries.

The evidence suggests a mixture of both. A December 2025 order for a dual MBE 6000 system placed by a European customer — representing two production units in a single transaction — inflated the European share mechanically, given that production systems carry multi-million-euro price tags. Yet the broader trend is reinforced by structural factors: European semiconductor policy, catalysed by the European Chips Act and national industrial strategies in France, Germany, and the Netherlands, has stimulated capital formation in compound-semiconductor manufacturing that is both insulated from US export-control risk and eligible for public co-funding. Research and academic procurement from European institutes, detailed below, adds a second layer of European revenue that is less lumpy and more reliably recurring. The North American recovery, driven primarily by the first two ROSIE commercial deliveries, is discussed in the silicon-photonics section.

## Universities and Institutes: The Recurring Research Customer Base

Riber's installed base of more than 800 systems worldwide was built one research laboratory at a time across five decades, and academic procurement remains a structural pillar of the business. Research-grade systems — smaller-footprint single- or multi-wafer cluster tools — typically carry price tags in the €500k–€2m range, meaningfully below production systems but spread across a larger and more geographically distributed customer population.

The roster Riber names in its public disclosures includes the University of Tokyo, Fraunhofer Institute (with multiple sites across Germany), IMEC in Belgium, Dongguk University in South Korea, and the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen via the NQCP partnership discussed below. These institutions procure through capital-equipment tender processes tied to government research grants, national laboratory framework contracts, and increasingly to defence-adjacent funding streams. Lead times from initial specification to contract award regularly exceed twelve months, but once awarded, academic relationships tend to generate long-duration aftermarket revenue: Riber's effusion cells, cracker sources, substrate manipulators, and in-situ monitoring tools wear and require periodic replacement, creating a parts-and-service attachment rate that extends the commercial lifetime of each initial sale well beyond equipment delivery.

The 2025 services-and-accessories segment decline of 7.8% — bringing that line to approximately €9.4m — was attributed in part to US government budgetary constraints that reduced procurement by American university laboratories. Federal budget pressures affected capital equipment purchasing across US research institutions in 2025, and Riber's relatively modest North American installed base magnified the impact on the services line. The recovery in North American systems revenue from ROSIE orders partially offset this drag at the top level, but the underlying academic procurement dynamic in the United States remained constrained through the frozen snapshot date.

## Defence Laboratories: Long Cycles, High Aftermarket Value

Government defence laboratories and classified-programme institutes constitute a segment that Riber addresses with research-grade systems for III-V infrared detector work — InAs/GaSb type-II superlattice and HgCdTe focal-plane arrays for night vision, space imaging, and missile-seeker applications — as well as nitride power-device research. These customers operate procurement cycles measured in years, routed through defence ministry capital programmes rather than commercial purchase orders, and often carry security constraints that limit public disclosure. Riber does not itemise defence laboratory revenue separately, but the segment is characterised by extremely high aftermarket attachment rates, given the classified operating environments that preclude switching to unfamiliar suppliers mid-programme, and by geopolitical resilience: European and North American defence laboratories are largely insulated from the export-licence risk that shadows Asian commercial orders.

## ROSIE Customers: The NQCP Partnership and the First US Order

The most strategically significant customer relationships established during the frozen dossier window are the two inaugural ROSIE orders. The first was placed by the Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme (NQCP), hosted at the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen, as the technology anchor of the POEM (Photonic Oxide Epitaxy Modulator Technology) initiative. The structure of POEM is instructive as a commercialisation template: NQCP contributes research expertise, pilot-line hosting infrastructure, and scientific credibility; Riber contributes the ROSIE system itself, a supply of BTO and STO thin-film samples on silicon wafers for distribution to third-party researchers beginning in 2026, and ongoing engineering support. The arrangement converts what might otherwise be a single academic sale into a commercial seeding mechanism — a reference installation backed by publication-grade characterisation data that lowers the adoption threshold for industrial customers evaluating BTO-on-silicon electro-optic modulator fabrication.

The second ROSIE order, announced in September 2025, came from a US-based quantum-computing company whose identity was not disclosed. The order confirmed North American commercial traction for BTO-on-silicon deposition and validated that ROSIE's 300 mm SEMI-compliant workflow — FOUP-to-FOUP automation, compatibility with existing CMOS fab infrastructure — was credible in an industrial rather than purely academic context. Together, these two orders account for ROSIE's entire commercial installed base through the frozen snapshot date.

## The Concentration Problem: Twelve Systems, Twelve Customers

With twelve MBE systems delivered to approximately twelve customers in fiscal 2025, Riber's revenue is structurally concentrated at the individual customer level in any given year. A single production-system delivery priced at €5–8m represents 12–20% of annual revenue in isolation; a dual-system order like the December 2025 European transaction represents a still larger share. Riber mitigates this through deposit and milestone-payment structures embedded in system contracts — customers pay staged instalments tied to manufacturing milestones, factory acceptance, and site delivery — which reduces cancellation exposure relative to a back-loaded payment model. Nonetheless, the deferral or cancellation of even one or two system orders carries material P&L consequence, as the semi-regular commentary on delayed Asian deliveries in Riber's public communications makes clear.

## The 2026 Order Book and Its Customer Signals

The order book entering 2026 at €26.9 million — up 24% year on year — comprises four production systems and one ROSIE unit. The January 2026 MBE 6000 order from a Japanese customer for quantum-dot laser fabrication targeting the datacom sector — specifically 1,300 nm quantum-dot lasers for 400G and 800G optical transceivers serving AI data-centre infrastructure — reaffirms Japan as a durable production-systems market and signals that AI-infrastructure build-out is beginning to translate into compound-semiconductor equipment demand with a tangible Riber footprint.

| End Market | 2025 Revenue Weight | Key Named Customers | Primary Geography |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compound-semiconductor foundries | Largest segment | IQE plc, Coherent/II-VI | Asia, Europe |
| Research universities and institutes | Mid-tier recurring | Fraunhofer, IMEC, Univ. Tokyo, Dongguk | Europe, Asia |
| Defence and government labs | Undisclosed | Unnamed European/NATO programmes | Europe, North America |
| Silicon photonics / quantum computing | Nascent (ROSIE) | NQCP/Niels Bohr, US quantum company | Europe, North America |
| Thin-film solar and OLED OEM | Services/accessories | Undisclosed | Global |
| Device start-ups and scale-ups | Sub-segment | Aledia, II-V Lab | Europe |

The aggregate picture that emerges is of a customer base undergoing a deliberate geographic and segment rebalancing. Asian foundry revenue — historically dominant but vulnerable to export controls — has contracted as a revenue share while European research, European production, and nascent North American ROSIE revenue have expanded. Whether the European surge sustains at 45% or represents partial timing artefact remains the central question for 2026 revenue delivery. The ROSIE platform, with its two named customers and a seeding strategy through BTO/STO sample distribution, is the vector most likely to structurally anchor North American and European revenue over the medium term — but it enters 2026 as a two-unit commercial programme against a 800-unit legacy installed base, and the distance between that starting point and material revenue contribution remains substantial.

chapters.title: Niche Dominance in a Three-Horse Race: Riber's Competitive Position Against Veeco, DCA, and the Silicon-Photonics Equipment Field
chapters.body:
## A Market Too Small to Attract Insurgents, Too Technical to Invite Amateurs

The global market for molecular beam epitaxy systems has long occupied a peculiar position in the semiconductor capital-equipment landscape: large enough to support three credible commercial manufacturers, too small and too technically demanding to attract the well-capitalised platform players that dominate adjacent deposition categories. Third-party estimates placed the MBE systems market at somewhere between $95 million and $296 million in the 2024–2026 period, a range so wide as to expose the fundamental difficulty of sizing a market where most transactions are privately negotiated, delivery schedules span twelve to eighteen months, and a single system order can shift a supplier's annual revenue by several percentage points. What the estimates agreed on was the growth trajectory: a compound annual rate of roughly 7–8%, driven by structural expansion in compound-semiconductor device production for 5G radio-frequency front ends, VCSEL arrays, quantum-dot lasers, and infrared detection systems.

Within that market, three manufacturers divided the commercially meaningful order flow. Riber SA, headquartered in Bezons and publicly listed on Euronext Growth Paris, held the largest installed base worldwide—more than 800 systems across university laboratories, national research institutes, defence establishments, and commercial epiwafer foundries. Veeco Instruments, listed on Nasdaq under the ticker VECO and generating approximately $600 million in annual revenues, maintained an MBE product line as a secondary offering within a broader portfolio centred on metal-organic chemical vapour deposition reactors for compound-LED and laser-diode production. DCA Instruments, a Finnish private company, served a predominantly academic and government-laboratory customer base with research-grade systems positioned at the lower-throughput, higher-customisation end of the market. Secondary participants—SVT Associates in the United States, Scienta Omicron GmbH in Germany, and the component specialist Dr. Eberl MBE-Komponenten GmbH—occupied further niches in surface-science MBE and consumable supply without competing for industrial production-system contracts.

The barriers to entry protecting all three incumbents were structural and compounding. Ultra-high-vacuum engineering at the 10⁻¹⁰ torr regime required decades of proprietary process knowledge in stainless-steel fabrication, cryogenic design, effusion-cell thermal management, and substrate-heating control. Customer reference-site requirements imposed an additional hurdle: a prospective buyer of a production MBE system—typically an epiwafer foundry committing several million euros of capital and entrusting its process roadmap to a single supplier—demanded evidence of comparable systems operating reliably at peer facilities. Without an installed base, a new entrant could not generate reference sites; without reference sites, it could not close production orders. The learning curve ran approximately a decade from first prototype to credible production-system supplier, a timeline long enough to deter all but the most strategically motivated challengers.

## Focus as Competitive Weapon: Riber Versus Veeco

The most important competitive dynamic in the production-system segment was less a battle between equals than a structural divergence in strategic attention. Veeco was, by the early 2020s, primarily a MOCVD equipment company. Its metal-organic CVD reactors supplied the LED and laser-diode manufacturing lines of Asian and European device makers, and this product line generated the majority of Veeco's revenue. MBE was retained in the Veeco portfolio but received a commensurately smaller share of engineering resource, sales force attention, and product-development investment.

Riber, by contrast, derived every euro of its €40.3 million in 2025 revenues from MBE systems, components, and associated aftermarket services. The entire organisation—its 119 employees, its Bezons R&D laboratories, its application MBE facility, its US and China subsidiaries—existed to advance one deposition technology. This focus differential manifested in measurable ways. Riber maintained a deeper catalogue of effusion-cell geometries, source configurations, and in-situ monitoring instruments than any competitor. Its service network, built around subsidiaries and regional distributors, could provide on-site support to customers across Europe, North America, and Asia with a response capability that a secondary product line within a larger company struggled to replicate. And its application laboratory in Bezons allowed Riber engineers to validate new material systems—oxides, nitrides, dilute nitrides, II-VI compounds—before customers committed capital, a pre-sales resource with no direct equivalent at Veeco's MBE division.

The consequence of this focus was customer lock-in that went beyond contractual terms. Process recipes developed on a Riber MBE 6000—the precise temperature ramp sequences, source flux calibrations, shutter timing protocols, and in-situ reflectometry baselines that defined a commercial epiwafer production process—were not readily portable to a competitor's machine. Switching costs included not just the capital cost of a replacement system but the engineering time to re-qualify the process, the yield risk during the transition period, and the retraining of operators familiar with Riber's software control environment. For a compound-semiconductor foundry supplying VCSEL wafers to a tier-one handset manufacturer on a just-in-time schedule, those switching costs were prohibitive. The result was that new production-system purchasers—particularly those adding capacity to an existing Riber-equipped line—overwhelmingly chose to remain with Riber, a loyalty dynamic that became self-reinforcing as the installed base grew.

## DCA Instruments: Adjacent Market, Not Direct Rival

DCA Instruments occupied a strategically distinct position that rendered it a partial rather than full competitor to Riber. The Finnish company's product line was concentrated in research-grade systems for academic physics and materials-science departments, government-funded laboratories, and the surface-science community. Its machines were optimised for flexibility, modularity, and the ability to accommodate exotic substrate geometries, cryogenic sample stages, and ultra-low-temperature characterisation environments—requirements that differed fundamentally from the multi-wafer throughput, automated cassette handling, and process repeatability that defined Riber's production-system customers.

Where direct competition occurred, it was at the boundary between pilot-scale research and early-stage production: a corporate R&D centre ordering its second or third MBE system, or a national institute beginning to expand into applied device prototyping. In these cases, DCA's customisation capability and Riber's production-system heritage competed on the same RFQ, with outcome typically determined by the customer's longer-term production intent. For customers with a clear path toward industrial-scale compound-semiconductor fabrication, Riber's production-system architecture and global service infrastructure provided a more compelling proposition; for those whose work would remain fundamentally academic, DCA's flexibility held appeal. The overlap was real but limited, and neither company appeared to have materially displaced the other in its primary domain.

## The Silicon-Photonics Arena: A Different Set of Rivals

The competitive landscape surrounding the ROSIE platform bore no resemblance to the three-horse MBE race. In silicon photonics, Riber was not competing against Veeco or DCA. It was entering a market historically served by CVD tool companies—Applied Materials, Lam Research, and their peers—with a deposition capability those companies did not offer.

The distinction was technical and consequential. Chemical vapour deposition of barium titanate on silicon produced films with structural disorder, oxygen vacancy defects, and interfacial roughness that degraded the electro-optic Pockels coefficient on which modulator performance depended. MBE-grown BTO, deposited by ROSIE's ultra-high-vacuum process at precisely controlled substrate temperatures and flux ratios, achieved epitaxial crystal quality—single-crystal, atomically coherent, with defect densities orders of magnitude lower than CVD counterparts—that translated directly into higher modulation efficiency, lower drive voltage, and reduced insertion loss in electro-optic modulator devices. No incumbent CVD supplier had demonstrated a production-capable alternative route to equivalent BTO film quality as of the frozen snapshot date.

This created a first-mover window. Riber's 2025 ROSIE orders—the NQCP/Niels Bohr Institute unit for the POEM pilot line in Denmark and the US quantum-computing company order announced in September 2025—were proof points of nascent commercial traction. The risk was explicit: Applied Materials, with a market capitalisation roughly one thousand times Riber's and an installed base spanning every advanced logic and memory fab on the planet, could in principle redirect a fraction of its process-integration engineering capability toward CVD-BTO development. If and when CVD-based BTO deposition achieved film quality comparable to MBE, Riber's competitive position in silicon photonics would narrow rapidly. The window was real; its duration was uncertain.

## Sizing the Moat

| Competitive Advantage | Basis | Durability Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Installed base (800+ systems) | Reference sites, aftermarket hooks, switching costs | High — compounding with each new delivery |
| Process-recipe IP | 60 years of MBE engineering across III-V, II-VI, oxide systems | High — tacit knowledge, not easily replicated |
| Global service network | Subsidiaries in US and China; regional distributors | Medium — replicable by a well-funded entrant with time |
| ROSIE first-mover (oxide-on-silicon MBE) | No incumbent CVD supplier offers equivalent BTO film quality | Medium — contingent on sustained CVD-BTO development lag |
| Focus premium over Veeco MBE | Entire organisation aligned to MBE; deeper catalogue, stronger support | Medium-high — structural but dependent on Veeco not investing |

Riber's installed-base density was its most durable competitive asset. Eight hundred systems distributed across every significant compound-semiconductor research institution and production facility worldwide meant that virtually every engineer trained on MBE equipment had learned on a Riber machine. The tacit knowledge embedded in that installed base—the collective memory of service histories, process optimisations, and material-system solutions accumulated across six decades—was not a database that a competitor could purchase or reverse-engineer. It was a network effect expressed in human capital, and it widened with every additional system delivered.

Riber's 2025 revenue of €40.3 million implied a market share in the range of 14–42% of the MBE systems market depending on the estimate used—a range too wide to be analytically satisfying but directionally consistent with market leadership. What the financials confirmed was that this leadership was becoming more profitable: gross margins of 38.6% in 2025 against approximately 34% two years earlier were evidence that the installed-base density and focus advantage were translating into pricing power, not merely volume. That combination—market leadership, accelerating margins, and a credible first-mover position in a new equipment category—was what the market, as of the frozen snapshot date, was only beginning to price in.

chapters.title: Timeline and Triggers: The News Catalysts That Have Shaped and Will Shape Riber SA
chapters.body:
## The Inflection That Built the Story: 2023–2024

The narrative arc of Riber SA's recent re-rating begins with a single revenue line reported in February 2024: full-year 2023 revenues of €39.2 million, up 41% from €27.8 million in fiscal 2022. The driver was unmistakable—MBE systems deliveries had nearly doubled, as a wave of compound-semiconductor capacity investment, buoyed by 5G RF front-end demand and nascent VCSEL expansion for AI-adjacent 3D sensing, pushed production-system orders through Riber's Bezons factory simultaneously. No restructuring, no acquisition, no subsidy—just order-book conversion.

The governance catalyst arrived six months earlier. In September 2023, the Supervisory Board accepted the resignation of its own president, Annie Geoffroy, and immediately installed her as President of the Management Board, the operational apex of Riber's then-dual governance structure. The move was quietly revolutionary: Geoffroy, a transition-management specialist trained at ESCP Europe with a DESS in Management Control, had spent years watching the company from the supervisory tier. Her elevation consolidated authority and signalled that the profitability programme she had been pressing for would now have executive teeth.

June 2024 hardened the governance shift into permanent architecture. At the Combined General Meeting on 19 June, shareholders voted to dissolve the dual Management Board/Supervisory Board framework entirely and create a seven-member unified Board of Directors under the MiddleNext Corporate Governance Code. Geoffroy was unanimously appointed Chairwoman and CEO, a combined role she has held since. The restructuring removed institutional friction and gave Riber a cleaner decision-making chain at the precise moment ROSIE was moving from laboratory curiosity to commercial project.

## The ROSIE Catalysts: First Orders, US Anchor

The announcement of the POEM initiative—a joint pilot line between Riber and the Niels Bohr Institute's Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme (NQCP) in Denmark—was the first external signal that the ROSIE platform had crossed from internal R&D to contracted commercial activity. The NQCP order, the first of two ROSIE units sold in 2025, committed Riber to delivering a 300 mm, SEMI-compliant BTO-on-silicon MBE system for H2 2025, and committed NQCP to establishing POEM as a reference pilot line for Pockels-effect electro-optic modulator development.

The second ROSIE catalyst landed in September 2025 and carried arguably greater strategic weight. A US-based quantum-computing company placed the second commercial ROSIE order, making it Riber's initial North American penetration in silicon photonics. The geopolitical significance is not subtle: US semiconductor equipment export controls—operating through the Commerce Department's Entity List and the Export Administration Regulations licence requirements—are the primary constraint on Riber's ability to ship advanced MBE systems to Chinese and certain other Asian customers. A US anchor customer is inherently export-licence-free. Every ROSIE unit sold domestically or to European and US counterparts sidesteps the regulatory friction that has carved €4 million from Riber's 2025 revenue. The US order does not solve the export-control problem, but it points toward a customer geography for ROSIE that is structurally insulated from it.

## The Export-Licence Rupture and Its Ongoing Shadow

Riber's 2025 annual results—full-year revenue disclosed in February 2026 and the complete P&L released in April 2026—contained the starkest single disclosure in the company's recent history: export licence refusals had blocked approximately €4 million of identifiable commercial opportunities during the year. Management's guidance for 2026 revenue growth was explicitly conditioned on obtaining the required export licences for identified pipeline orders. The language amounts to a public admission that a binary regulatory variable is embedded in the forward revenue model.

The regulatory framework at issue is the US Export Administration Regulations, which extend jurisdiction to foreign-made equipment containing US-origin technology or software above de minimis thresholds—a category that encompasses sophisticated MBE systems with American-sourced control software, vacuum components, or characterisation tools. When a potential Chinese or sanctioned-entity customer appears on the Entity List, Riber must apply for a US licence before shipping; refusal means the order is lost, not deferred. In 2025, those refusals cost the company the equivalent of roughly 10% of MBE systems revenues.

The probability-weighted impact on 2026 guidance is material. The order book entering 2026 stood at €26.9 million, up 24%, and management described four contracted production systems plus one ROSIE unit. If even one or two of those production-system orders require licences that are denied, 2026 revenues could fall short of consensus expectations regardless of operational execution. Geoffroy's conditional guidance language is not boilerplate—it is a direct acknowledgement that this catalyst is binary and not within management's control.

## The December 2025 and January 2026 System Orders

Two additional catalyst events in the quarter straddling year-end 2025 reinforced the production-system order narrative. In December 2025, Riber announced receipt of an order for two MBE 6000 production systems from a European customer—customer identity undisclosed, system type production-grade, geography European. The dual-system structure of the order is commercially notable: a customer procuring two units simultaneously is almost certainly a compound-semiconductor epiwafer foundry scaling capacity rather than a research institution ordering a single tool. Lead times on MBE 6000 systems typically run six to twelve months, suggesting that December 2025 delivery schedule targets point toward H2 2026 revenue recognition, reinforcing the back-half concentration pattern already observed in 2024 and 2025.

In January 2026, a Japanese customer placed a separate MBE 6000 order for quantum-dot laser fabrication destined for datacom optical transceivers operating at 1,300 nm—a wavelength critical to the 400G and 800G pluggable modules proliferating in AI data-centre switching fabrics. The order underlines that ROSIE is additive to the MBE 6000 franchise rather than substitutive: Japan remains a recurring production-systems market, and demand there is being driven by the same AI infrastructure build-out that makes ROSIE's silicon-photonics proposition compelling to US customers.

## The Four Forward Catalysts for 2026

| Catalyst | Nature | Binary? | Timing | Revenue at Stake |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Export-licence grants on pipeline orders | Regulatory | Yes | Rolling; H1/H2 2026 | ~€4m+ if 2025 pattern repeats |
| ROSIE 2 manufacturing completion & acceptance | Operational | Partial | 2026 delivery | New ASP tier; re-rates ROSIE TAM |
| BTO/STO sample availability & ecosystem seeding | Commercial development | No | 2026 onwards | Pipeline velocity indicator |
| H1 2026 revenue release | Financial | No | ~August 2026 | Tests H1 2025 trough recurrence |

The export-licence catalyst is the most acute. A grant enables €4-plus million in revenue that is already in the order book; a refusal removes it, potentially repeating 2025's drag.

ROSIE 2—a dual-chamber cluster system designed for higher wafer-per-hour throughput—is the manufacturing proof-of-concept investors need before the platform can be sized seriously in any valuation model. First-generation ROSIE units validate the chemistry and the customer proposition; ROSIE 2 validates that Riber can build a production-capable tool for industrial foundry workflows.

The BTO/STO sample distribution programme, part of the POEM initiative, functions as a commercial seeding operation: by placing thin-film samples with photonics research groups and device-start-ups in 2026, Riber populates a funnel of potential ROSIE customers who need to evaluate the material before ordering a system. Sample availability is a leading indicator of ROSIE order velocity twelve to eighteen months hence.

## The June 2026 AGM: Near-Term Corporate Catalyst

The Annual General Meeting, scheduled for June 17, 2026, carries three agenda items with market relevance. First, the approval and payment of the €0.10 per share dividend—payable June 24, 2026—represents a 25% increase over the prior year and signals that the board views the FY 2025 profitability inflection as durable rather than opportunistic. Second, any board composition changes or refreshment will be watched against the MiddleNext governance framework the company adopted only two years prior. Third, and most consequential for investors, management typically uses the AGM forum to update or affirm medium-term strategic objectives—particularly around ROSIE commercialisation milestones and 2026 full-year revenue guidance conditionality. Given that H1 2026 results will not be public at the AGM date, any qualitative commentary Geoffroy offers on order-book conversion progress, export-licence status, and ROSIE 2 timeline will move directly into market pricing of a stock that, having appreciated approximately 384% in the preceding twelve months, has priced in considerable optimism that management must now begin to convert into reported numbers.

chapters.title: Process IP, Published Research, and the R&D Engine Behind MBE Leadership
chapters.body:
## A Different Kind of Moat

For most semiconductor capital-equipment companies, intellectual property means a bulging patent portfolio and an army of licensing attorneys. Riber SA's moat is built differently. As a maker of ultra-high-vacuum systems serving scientific communities that publish, peer-review, and openly discuss materials physics, Riber has long understood that the durable competitive barriers in molecular beam epitaxy reside less in registered claims than in accumulated know-how that is extraordinarily difficult to replicate without decades of hands-on system-building experience.

The company almost certainly holds formal IP in system architecture—the geometric arrangement of source flanges, effusion-cell mounting angles, and cryogenic shroud configurations that define the MBE 6000 and MBE 7000 reactors—as well as in the control algorithms governing source temperature ramping, flux stabilisation, and substrate rotation. Innovations in effusion-cell design, particularly the valved cracker sources and high-temperature cells acquired through the 2004 Addon transaction, likely carry additional registered protection. But the deeper competitive asset is what the patent register cannot contain: the calibration procedures, growth recipes, beam-equivalent-pressure profiles, and source conditioning sequences that Riber's application-laboratory engineers have refined across more than sixty years and eight hundred installed systems. That corpus of process know-how, embedded in the institutional memory of a small team in Bezons, is the true substrate of MBE market leadership.

## The Application Laboratory as Commercial Asset

Riber operates an in-house application MBE laboratory at its Bezons headquarters where compound-semiconductor growth experiments are conducted on research-grade equipment. This facility serves a dual function that is underappreciated in standard product-company analysis. On one hand, it is the R&D engine through which new deposition processes—including the BTO and STO oxide films central to the ROSIE platform—are validated before customer delivery. On the other, it is a qualification and demonstration tool: prospective customers can run their own growth recipes on Riber hardware, evaluate crystal quality through X-ray diffraction and photoluminescence, and leave with process data that reduces integration risk. In an industry where a single system purchase commits a research budget for a decade, that hands-on qualification function is a meaningful sales accelerant.

Precise R&D expenditure as a share of revenue is not separately disclosed in the available Riber financial record with the granularity applied by listed peers such as Veeco Instruments, which in recent years has reported R&D intensity of roughly 10–12% of revenues. For a 119-person company generating approximately €40m in annual revenue, an R&D head count of 20–30 engineers is a plausible estimate, translating to an R&D cost envelope—salaries, equipment depreciation, consumables—that likely falls in the 8–12% of revenue range. What is clear from the statutory accounts is that Riber's operating cost structure supported a 38.6% gross margin and a 12.7% operating margin in fiscal 2025, implying that R&D investment has been held in careful proportion to revenue rather than scaled aggressively ahead of ROSIE commercialisation.

## MBE Control Solutions and the Software Layer

The 2015 acquisition of MBE Control Solutions, a US-based firm, was framed publicly as a deepening of Riber's automation software capability for the North American research market. Its more durable significance lies in what it contributed to the control-system architecture that now underpins Riber's production platforms and, critically, the ROSIE platform's SEMI-compliant automation stack. A modern production MBE system differentiated from a research tool not primarily by the vacuum hardware but by the reliability, repeatability, and remote-monitoring capability of its software. Uptime—measured over the ten-plus month continuous operating cycles the MBE 6000 is certified to sustain—is as much a software achievement as a mechanical one. The MBE Control Solutions IP, integrated into Riber's standard software suite over the decade since acquisition, is therefore a latent competitive differentiator that surfaces most visibly in customer qualification reviews comparing Riber production systems against Veeco alternatives.

## EZ-CURVE and EZ-REF: Aftermarket IP with Recurring Revenue Characteristics

Riber's in-situ monitoring product lines—EZ-CURVE, which measures real-time wafer curvature as a proxy for epitaxial stress, and EZ-REF, a reflectometry tool that tracks surface reconstruction and deposition rate in situ—represent a distinct IP cluster with meaningful commercial optionality. Sold both as factory-integrated options on new systems and as retrofit upgrades to the worldwide installed base, these tools address a persistent customer need: the ability to monitor and intervene in a growth run without breaking vacuum and destroying the wafer. The sensor geometries, optical configurations, and the data-interpretation algorithms that convert raw curvature or reflectometry signals into actionable process feedback are the protectable core. As a retrofit product addressing more than eight hundred installed Riber systems, EZ-CURVE and EZ-REF represent a recurring-revenue opportunity anchored in an installed base that Riber owns by virtue of its market position.

## The POEM IP Architecture and Open-Science Seeding

The POEM (Photonic Oxide Epitaxy Modulator Technology) initiative with NQCP at the Niels Bohr Institute carries an IP structure that is notably asymmetric in its strategic logic. Joint academic-industrial collaborations of this type typically allocate foreground IP—innovations arising from the collaboration—on a negotiated basis, with equipment-process IP remaining with the industrial partner and device-architecture insights often shared or jointly owned. Riber's decision to make BTO and STO thin-film samples on silicon available to the broader scientific community beginning in 2026 reads not as naivety about competitive disclosure but as a deliberate ecosystem-seeding strategy: the more device engineers across photonics start-ups and integrated-photonics foundries have hands-on experience with Riber-grown oxide films, the larger the funnel for eventual ROSIE system purchases.

## The Road Ahead: Scale, ROSIE 2, and the Veeco Question

The forward R&D agenda is defined by the transition from demonstration to production. ROSIE 2, the dual-chamber cluster version planned for manufacturing in 2026, addresses the throughput constraint that limits ROSIE's addressability to pilot-scale customers. Process optimisation of BTO and STO growth on 300 mm silicon—targeting the layer-to-layer repeatability and defect densities required for commercial electro-optic modulator fabrication—remains ongoing. Longer-term, extension to lithium niobate (LiNbO₃) and lanthanum-doped BTO, both materials with established electro-optic credentials, would widen ROSIE's functional scope.

The genuine strategic tension is one of scale. With approximately 119 employees total and an estimated 20–30 in R&D, Riber's technical workforce is a fraction of Veeco's. Maintaining MBE leadership against a larger competitor while simultaneously developing an entirely new platform in oxide silicon photonics is an allocation problem with no comfortable answer. What Riber has—and what no competitor can easily acquire—is sixty years of accumulated process knowledge and an installed base that generates both aftermarket revenues and the iterative application-laboratory feedback loop that turns equipment failures and customer growth anomalies into IP. That institutional knowledge base, more than any patent filing, is the foundation on which the ROSIE bet is being placed.

chapters.title: Six Risks That Could Derail Riber's ROSIE Bet and Profitability Inflection
chapters.body:
The profitability inflection Riber delivered in fiscal 2025—net income up 27.1% to €5.2 million, gross margin at a record 38.6%, order book entering 2026 up 24% to €26.9 million—was a genuine structural achievement for a company of fewer than 120 employees. But each pillar of that achievement rests on assumptions that carry material downside. Six risks, taken individually or in combination, could slow or reverse the trajectory that equity investors appear to have priced at a 384% one-year share appreciation through May 2026.

## Risk 1: Export Licence Uncertainty

MBE production systems are dual-use capital goods governed by overlapping regulatory regimes: the United States Export Administration Regulations (EAR) control re-export by non-US entities of items incorporating US-origin technology; the French dual-use export framework implements EU Regulation 2021/821; and the Wassenaar Arrangement, to which France is a signatory, coordinates multilateral controls on advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Riber's MBE 6000 and MBE 7000 systems, which operate under ultra-high-vacuum conditions to deposit precision compound-semiconductor films, fall within the compound-semiconductor equipment classifications subject to national-security review when the end-user is domiciled in jurisdictions of concern—principally mainland China, but increasingly certain research institutions elsewhere.

The quantified cost in 2025 was €4 million of revenue blocked by licence refusals on identified commercial opportunities. Against a €40.3 million revenue base, that represents a 9.9% top-line drag that Riber absorbed without public complaint but could not fully offset. More significantly, the company's guidance for 2026 revenue growth is explicitly conditional on obtaining required export licences—a formulation unusual in industrial equipment guidance and one that acknowledges regulatory discretion as a material swing variable outside management control.

The scenario math is instructive. If two additional systems—each averaging approximately €2.5 million based on disclosed deliveries and revenue per system ratios—are denied licences in 2026, the direct revenue shortfall approaches €5 million. At production-systems gross margins that have improved with mix, the gross-profit loss likely exceeds €2 million, and after operating-cost absorption, the impact on operating income—which reached only €5.1 million in 2025—could represent a 30–40% earnings headwind on a stable cost base. The fixed-cost manufacturing facility in Bezons does not scale down proportionately with a short-cycle revenue shortfall.

| Scenario | Blocked Revenue | Est. Gross Profit Impact | Est. Operating Income 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base (no additional refusals) | €0m | €0m | ~€5.5–6.0m |
| One additional system denied | ~€2.5m | ~€1.0m | ~€4.5–5.0m |
| Two additional systems denied | ~€5.0m | ~€2.0m | ~€3.5–4.0m |

The regulatory environment has tightened, not eased, since 2025. Successive rounds of US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) entity-list expansions and the broadening of advanced-manufacturing equipment controls to cover more semiconductor deposition categories make it prudent to assume that the licence-refusal rate is unlikely to fall materially in the near term.

## Risk 2: Asian Customer Concentration and Geopolitical Disruption

Asia's share of Riber's revenues fell from 57.3% in 2024 to 39.7% in 2025, a diversification that CEO Annie Geoffroy welcomed. But 39.7% of a €40 million revenue base—approximately €16 million—remains concentrated in a geography facing the sharpest semiconductor trade-control escalation in a generation. Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and China collectively constitute Riber's largest regional customer pool for production-system orders. Each carries distinct geopolitical risk.

Taiwan's compound-semiconductor foundries and vertically integrated VCSEL producers represent potentially the most commercially valuable but geopolitically sensitive customer set. Any expansion of US or EU export controls to cover advanced deposition tools supplied to Taiwan-based entities would challenge Riber's ability to service contracts already in negotiation. South Korean research universities and GaAs/InP producers face analogous scrutiny as allied governments debate how broadly to apply semiconductor equipment controls beyond China. Japan, which placed an MBE 6000 quantum-dot laser order in January 2026, is today a relatively unconstrained market, but Japanese dual-use export policy has historically mirrored US BIS guidance with a lag.

The structural vulnerability is the fixed-cost manufacturing base in Bezons. Riber's 119 employees, its cleanroom fabrication capability, its ultra-high-vacuum assembly infrastructure—these costs do not reduce proportionately if Asian production-system orders decelerate. A scenario in which Asian revenues contract from €16 million to €10 million over two years, mirroring the trajectory of a second-order tightening of semiconductor equipment controls, would require European and North American order volumes to nearly double just to hold revenue flat. Given current European order cadence and the nascent state of ROSIE commercial revenue, that substitution is not guaranteed.

## Risk 3: ROSIE Commercialisation Execution Risk

With only two units ordered as of the frozen snapshot—one to NQCP in Denmark for the POEM pilot line, one to an undisclosed US quantum-computing company in September 2025—ROSIE is pre-revenue-significant. The platform's commercial thesis rests on three assumptions, each of which is falsifiable.

The first is technical: that barium titanate deposition on 300 mm silicon at the quality levels demonstrated on the POEM pilot line can be reproduced consistently in customer fabs at production volumes. MBE of ferroelectric oxides on silicon is technically demanding; BTO films are sensitive to interfacial oxide quality, substrate temperature uniformity, and source flux stability at scales that single-wafer research systems tolerate more easily than 300 mm production tools. Yield loss at the customer site in early commercial deployments could delay repeat orders or trigger warranty-return cycles that absorb engineering bandwidth Riber can ill afford at its scale.

The second assumption is competitive: that chemical vapour deposition (CVD) or atomic layer deposition (ALD) based approaches to electro-optic modulator fabrication do not achieve comparable Pockels-effect device performance before ROSIE establishes an installed base. Applied Materials, Lam Research, and Tokyo Electron collectively invest in R&D at multiples of Riber's annual revenue; if any of these companies direct meaningful engineering effort toward oxide EO modulator deposition, they could bring alternative solutions to silicon-photonics foundries faster than Riber can scale its customer ecosystem.

The third assumption is temporal: that silicon-photonics foundries and hyperscaler photonics procurement teams make ROSIE adoption decisions before broader industry standardisation of oxide electro-optic platforms is established. Foundries investing in new deposition tool platforms require conviction that the underlying device architecture will be adopted by multiple device designers. If the industry coalesces around silicon-nitride or lithium-niobate-on-insulator modulators rather than BTO-on-silicon, ROSIE's addressable market shrinks materially before it has generated meaningful revenue.

## Risk 4: Revenue Lumpiness and Working Capital Strain

Riber's fiscal cadence is structurally skewed: H1 2025 revenues were €10.7 million, representing only 26.6% of the full-year total, while H2 delivered €29.5 million. This back-half concentration reflects the long lead times, factory acceptance tests, and customer-site readiness milestones embedded in MBE system deliveries. For an equity market accustomed to quarterly reporting, the pattern creates a first-half P&L that looks operationally troubled before full-year conversion makes the picture coherent.

The working-capital implications compound the communications challenge. Large production systems typically require advance payments that create deferred-revenue liabilities and tie up customer capital before delivery; conversely, Riber must invest in long-lead UHV components and precision machining well ahead of cash receipt. The €7.5 million cash balance at December 31, 2025—down from €8.6 million a year earlier—provides a modest liquidity buffer, but a scenario in which two or three H1 2026 deliveries are deferred by customer-capex contraction or export-licence delays could push the cash position toward levels requiring either credit-facility activation or dividend suspension.

Order cancellations, while historically infrequent in specialised capital equipment, are not unknown in customer-capex contraction cycles. The €26.9 million order book entering 2026 provides comfort, but its concentration in a small number of large-ticket items means that a single cancellation or multi-quarter deferral could shift the full-year revenue outcome by 6–8% without warning.

## Risk 5: Key-Person Dependency and Succession

Annie Geoffroy is approximately 70 years old. She holds the combined Chairwoman and CEO role, having arrived at Riber as a transition manager before her appointment to the Management Board in September 2023. No successor has been publicly identified. No separate CFO has been named in Riber's investor-relations materials. The board's five independent directors—including the academically credentialed Nicolas Grandjean and four others—provide oversight but are unlikely to substitute for Geoffroy's operational continuity in export-compliance negotiations, ROSIE commercialisation strategy, and customer relationships that have been cultivated under her tenure.

The governance code applicable to Riber—the MiddleNext Code for smaller listed companies—permits the combined Chair/CEO structure but recommends dissociation above certain size thresholds. The absence of a disclosed succession plan is not unusual for a French micro-cap, but it represents a material risk given the concentration of strategic momentum in a single individual approaching a natural transition point. A CEO transition at this specific juncture—mid-ROSIE commercialisation, mid-export-licence negotiation, mid-margin-improvement programme—would create uncertainty across all three strategic threads simultaneously. The institutional memory and regulator relationships accumulated through Geoffroy's tenure are not trivially transferable.

## Risk 6: Scale Constraint Against Well-Funded Competitors

Riber employs approximately 119 people. Veeco Instruments, its closest publicly listed peer, employs thousands across its compound-semiconductor and silicon-technology equipment divisions and generated revenues of approximately $600 million in its most recent fiscal year—roughly fifteen times Riber's scale. The asymmetry in R&D budget, field-service engineering headcount, application-laboratory capacity, and sales-force reach is correspondingly severe.

In the core MBE market, Riber's installed-base advantage of more than 800 systems worldwide and its deep institutional relationships in III-V research provide genuine competitive insulation. Veeco has not historically prioritised MBE as a growth vector. But the silicon-photonics opportunity changes the competitive calculus. If BTO-on-silicon electro-optic modulator deposition emerges as a validated production process—validated in part by Riber's own POEM pilot line—larger tool companies will notice. Veeco could acquire DCA Instruments of Finland or another MBE specialist to accelerate entry into oxide epitaxy. Applied Materials, already supplying CVD and ALD tools to the foundries ROSIE targets, could invest in an MBE capability that leverages its existing customer relationships.

Riber's ability to develop ROSIE 2, expand its applications laboratory, support customer qualifications at multiple sites simultaneously, and iterate the platform toward higher wafer-per-hour output is constrained by headcount and capital in ways that a better-funded entrant is not. The window of competitive isolation in oxide MBE is real but not indefinite, and Riber's 119-person organisation will need to execute without margin for error to convert its first-mover position into a defensible platform franchise before larger players develop credible alternatives.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Setup at the Frozen Snapshot

Riber entered the twelve months following May 23, 2026 with its clearest order-book visibility in recent memory and its most consequential strategic test since the 1994 decision to concentrate entirely on MBE. The backlog stood at €26.9 million at the start of fiscal 2026—up 24% from the prior opening position—comprising four contracted production systems and one ROSIE unit, providing the H2-loaded revenue cover that the company's structural delivery cadence reliably converts into full-year earnings. Against that constructive position, two variables dominated the outlook: whether French export authorities released the licences blocking an estimated €4 million in Asian opportunities, and whether the ROSIE platform generated additional order intake that extended the pipeline beyond its contracted deliveries.

> "2025 was an important milestone for RIBER, with a significant improvement in our profitability and the first commercial successes of our ROSIE platform," Chairwoman and CEO Annie Geoffroy said in presenting the [full-year 2025 results](https://www.riber.com/financial_documents/riber-delivers-strong-earnings-growth-in-2025/).

That statement, made in early 2026 against a backdrop of 53% cumulative net-income growth since fiscal 2023 on essentially flat revenues, compressed the entire investment question into a single sentence: profitability had inflected; the commercial question was whether ROSIE would now amplify it.

## The Catalyst Calendar

Five discrete events carried material thesis implications across the twelve-month window.

**June 2026 — Annual General Meeting.** Riber's AGM for fiscal year 2025 fell in June, at which shareholders voted on the proposed €0.10-per-share dividend—a 25% increase over the prior year—and heard Geoffroy address the strategic agenda for 2026. The AGM statement represented the year's fullest formal articulation of management priorities and was the first scheduled opportunity after the frozen snapshot to hear updated language on export-licence status, ROSIE unit pipeline, and ROSIE 2 delivery timing.

**July–August 2026 — H1 2026 Preliminary Revenue.** Riber's practice of releasing preliminary revenue figures in advance of full half-year accounts produced a first hard data point on order-book conversion. H1 is structurally light—H1 2025 delivered only €10.7 million, representing 26.6% of the full year—so the absolute figure would not be informative about the annual outcome in isolation. What mattered was whether H1 2026 tracked materially above H1 2025, which would imply either a ROSIE unit recorded in the first half or an unusually front-loaded production-system schedule. Any H1 revenue above €12 million would constitute positive evidence of delivery pull-forward.

**September–October 2026 — H1 2026 Full Results.** The half-year report would release gross margin data—the primary operating metric to track in the Geoffroy era. The progression from 36.1% in 2024 to 38.6% in 2025 had been the defining financial narrative of her tenure; whether 2026 sustained the trajectory toward 39–40% was the single most informative indicator of mix and pricing discipline holding under a post-rerating valuation.

**Q3–Q4 2026 — ROSIE 2 Manufacturing Completion.** Riber confirmed in its [April 2026 earnings release](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news_items/2026/apr/riber-100426.shtml) that the dual-chamber ROSIE 2 cluster tool was entering manufacturing during the year. A press release confirming first-article completion, initial customer qualification, or a ROSIE 2 order would constitute a discrete re-rating catalyst, expanding the addressable throughput of the platform and making oxide-on-silicon MBE viable for customers requiring production-scale rather than pilot-scale deposition rates.

**February–April 2027 — FY 2026 Preliminary and Full Results.** The most consequential release in the window, expected in the pattern established by the February–April 2026 cadence for fiscal 2025. This announcement would determine whether the 24% order-book growth at year-start translated into visible revenue expansion or was partially neutralised by export-licence attrition for a second consecutive fiscal year.

## Revenue and Earnings Implied by the Order Book

Riber carried minimal sell-side coverage—its Euronext Growth Paris listing, approximately 21.25 million shares outstanding, and sub-€50 million revenue base precluded a formal analyst consensus—so the relevant reference was management guidance and order-book arithmetic rather than a Bloomberg aggregate.

[Riber's investor relations disclosures](https://www.riber.com/finance/) stated that the 2026 revenue outlook was "conditioned on obtaining the required export licences," a formulation that acknowledged the binary nature of the Asian segment. Working from the €26.9 million opening order book and the structural services-and-accessories run rate of approximately €9–10 million annually—anchored by the 800-plus-unit worldwide installed base—the mathematics of full-year fiscal 2026 revenue resolved to a range of approximately €41–46 million.

| Scenario | FY 2026 Revenue | Growth vs. FY 2025 | Net Margin | Net Income | EPS (21.25m shares) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull: licences granted + third ROSIE order | €45–46m | +12–14% | 14–15% | €6.3–6.9m | €0.30–0.32 |
| Base: licences granted, no new ROSIE order | €42–44m | +5–9% | 13.5–14% | €5.7–6.2m | €0.27–0.29 |
| Bear: licences blocked ≥€4m again | €39–41m | −3–+2% | 12–13% | €4.7–5.3m | €0.22–0.25 |

Against the fiscal 2025 base of €0.245 per share in net income, the base-case envelope implied modest earnings compounding of 10–18%. The bull case approached 30–33% earnings per share growth—a figure that would require licence relief and the commercial confirmation of ROSIE as a repeatable product line rather than a two-unit pilot.

H1 2026 was unlikely to deliver a meaningful earnings signal. The business's structural H2-weighting—73% of fiscal 2025 revenue fell in the second half—meant the first-half result should be held lightly. The relevant H1 watchpoint was gross margin rather than revenue level.

## What to Watch Each Quarter

Three metrics bore watching with particular discipline in each reporting period across the window.

**Gross margin.** The 450-basis-point expansion from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 was achieved through production-system mix management and aftermarket pricing discipline. Any gross margin print below 38% in the H1 2026 report would signal either an unfavourable product mix—more research systems, fewer production tools—or price concessions in accessories. Gross margin above 39.5% would confirm that ROSIE's premium positioning and production-system ASP discipline were intact and that the margin inflection was structural rather than cyclical.

**ROSIE order count.** Units one and two were contracted in 2025—the first with [NQCP at the Niels Bohr Institute](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news_items/2026/feb/riber-030226.shtml) in Denmark and the second with a US quantum-computing company in September 2025. Unit three—whether for silicon photonics, quantum computing, or another oxide-on-silicon application—was the confirmation that ROSIE had crossed from prototype to commercial product line. A twelve-month window ending May 2027 with no third ROSIE order would constitute evidence that commercial seeding was slower than thesis.

**Order book trajectory.** The opening €26.9 million had to be replenished with new bookings as 2026 deliveries were recognised. An order book exiting fiscal 2026 above €28–30 million would provide meaningful cover for 2027 revenue growth. A book falling below €22 million would signal system demand cooling and raise the prospect of a 2027 revenue step-down.

## Beat and Miss Defined

Against the base-case envelope, a beat in fiscal 2026 required: full-year revenue above €44 million, at least one additional ROSIE order announced during the year, export licences granted on the blocked Asian volume, and gross margin clearing 39%. All four criteria clearing simultaneously would likely constitute a material re-rating event for a stock that had already appreciated approximately 384% in the preceding twelve months.

A miss would be confirmed by: full-year revenue below €41 million implying export headwinds equal to or worse than fiscal 2025, no new ROSIE orders through year-end, and gross margin stagnation or regression below 38%—which would suggest either mix deterioration or pricing pressure in the services segment recovering from its 7.8% decline in 2025.

## The Asymmetry at the Frozen Snapshot

The bull case rested on convergence: export-licence relief restoring Asian volume, ROSIE 2 shipping and generating a third commercial order, and gross-margin expansion toward 40% delivering net-income compounding well above revenue. A market capitalisation in the range of €300 million against base-case earnings of roughly €6 million implied a multiple approaching 50 times—a premium that priced in successful ROSIE commercialisation as an expectation, not as option value.

The bear case required no dramatic deterioration: a second consecutive year of €4 million-plus in blocked Asian revenue, no third ROSIE order, and gross-margin stagnation would produce earnings flat to modestly below fiscal 2025 and expose the multiple to sharp compression toward the 15–20 times range appropriate for a micro-cap industrial equipment supplier with a concentrated order book.

The asymmetry was thus characteristic of a platform-transition moment. The downside was a re-rating toward a more conventional industrial micro-cap multiple. The upside was the emergence of a credible silicon-photonics equipment franchise whose total addressable market—300 mm fab-compatible oxide deposition for AI datacentre interconnects—was orders of magnitude larger than its present revenue base. At the frozen snapshot, the market had already begun pricing the upside. The next twelve months would begin adjudicating whether the confidence was warranted.

chapters.title: 2026–2030: The Five-Year Horizon for Riber SA's ROSIE Scale-Up, Margin Maturation, and Market Expansion
chapters.body:
## The 2026 Setup: Order Book, Scenarios, and the Licence Variable

The €26.9 million order book Riber entered 2026 with — six contracted systems plus services, up 24 percent year-on-year — provided the most substantial forward revenue visibility the company had assembled in years. Two subsequent additions widened that base before the reporting period closed: a Japanese MBE 6000 order for quantum-dot laser fabrication announced in January 2026, and a European dual-system order received in December 2025. Together, these tranches implied a 2026 revenue range that management did not publicly quantify but that analytical triangulation could sketch.

Under a base case — stable licence approvals, normal H2 system-acceptance cadence — full-year 2026 revenues were plausibly headed toward €42–45 million, modestly above the €40.3 million posted in 2025. Four production systems, one ROSIE unit, and roughly flat services revenue produced high-single-digit growth on the arithmetic alone. An optimistic scenario, contingent on export-licence grants for the blocked Asian pipeline — the €4 million of 2025 revenue contractually identified but prevented from shipping — pushed the upper bound toward €46–48 million. The pessimistic case — additional refusals deepening the Asian revenue drought — held revenues close to flat at €39–41 million, with the H2 swing dependent almost entirely on European deliveries.

The structural variable management could not control was regulatory. Riber's 2026 growth guidance was explicitly conditioned on obtaining required export licences, and in an environment where the United States and European Union were progressively tightening semiconductor equipment controls, Riber's position as the dominant global MBE supplier to Asian foundries placed it squarely inside that policy perimeter.

## ROSIE: Projecting the Scale-Up Curve

The more consequential question for Riber's medium-term earnings trajectory was the rate at which ROSIE — the RIBER Oxide on Silicon Epitaxy platform — could accumulate commercial orders beyond its initial two units. The economics were materially different from the MBE 6000 base business.

In 2025, twelve MBE systems generated €30.9 million, implying a blended ASP of approximately €2.6 million. That blended figure obscured significant dispersion between research and production configurations. A standalone MBE 6000 for an Asian epiwafer foundry likely commanded €3.5–4.5 million. ROSIE, designed for 300 mm silicon wafers with SEMI FOUP-to-FOUP automation and targeting a domain in which no incumbent CMOS equipment supplier offered a competing oxide MBE solution, should command a novelty and engineering premium. ROSIE ASPs in the €5–7 million range — 25 to 60 percent above the MBE 6000 production configuration — were a defensible planning assumption.

| ROSIE Units/Year | ASP €5m Revenue | ASP €7m Revenue |
|---|---|---|
| 2 units (2026 base) | €10m | €14m |
| 3 units (2027) | €15m | €21m |
| 5 units (2028) | €25m | €35m |

Three to five ROSIE units annually by 2027–2028 was ambitious but grounded. The POEM pilot line at NQCP was engineered precisely to generate the validated electro-optic modulator data — wafer-level performance, defect density, thermal stability — that prospective silicon-photonics foundry customers would require before committing to a capital purchase. ROSIE 2, the dual-chamber cluster version entering manufacturing in 2026, addressed the higher-throughput industrial segment whose adoption could close faster once a reference tool was operational and generating published results.

## Margin Levers and the 40–42 Percent Threshold

The profitability inflection under Annie Geoffroy — 450 basis points of gross-margin expansion across 2023–2025 — was not exhausted. At 38.6 percent in 2025, the logical destination given available levers was a range of 40–42 percent by 2027–2028.

Three mechanisms drove the trajectory. First, ROSIE mix: units carrying ASPs 30–60 percent above the blended MBE 6000 average, and priced with limited competitive pressure on a novel platform, should contribute higher gross margins than the production-systems average. Second, overhead absorption at Bezons: the manufacturing footprint appeared adequate for current scale, meaning incremental ROSIE builds would absorb fixed costs without proportionate additions. Third, accessories pricing discipline: the global installed base of more than 800 systems compounded the recurring revenue opportunity in effusion cells, sources, and service contracts, and management had demonstrated the willingness to price that segment at premium rates.

At 40–42 percent gross margin and roughly stable selling and administrative costs, operating margin could reach 15–17 percent by 2028 — generating operating income of €7–9 million on a €45–55 million revenue base. Net income approaching €7–9 million would represent a 35–70 percent cumulative increase from 2025's €5.2 million without requiring revenue heroics.

## Secular Tailwinds: Four Forces Through 2030

Four structural end-market trends underpinned the demand side. 5G and 6G radio-frequency expansion continued to drive volume demand for GaN and GaAs HEMT epiwafers across Asia-Pacific foundries. The transition toward 6G millimetre-wave architectures, requiring higher-frequency transistors with sharper heterointerfaces, was likely to favour MBE over MOCVD for specific HEMT geometries.

AI data-centre optical interconnect was the fastest-growing vector. Quantum-dot lasers at 1,300 nm — the application underpinning the January 2026 Japan MBE 6000 order — were ascending as the preferred light source for co-packaged optics in hyperscaler switching at 800G and 1.6T. Every major silicon-photonics platform required a laser source that MBE-grown quantum-dot structures uniquely delivered, a structural alignment between Riber's core production capability and the AI infrastructure build-out.

Quantum computing hardware was a nascent but disproportionately high-value end market. Both ROSIE customers — NQCP and the unnamed US quantum-computing company — were quantum-hardware developers, not photonics fabs. This pointed to BTO-on-silicon as an electro-optic interface layer in quantum photonic processors, an application where MBE precision was architecturally required and no substitutable tool existed. Defence and space infrared detector programmes — procuring InAs/GaSb and HgCdTe type-II superlattice focal-plane arrays — provided long-cycle but geopolitically resilient demand, supported by post-2022 European defence spending increases and US military sensor procurement.

## The POEM Seeding Play: Customers by 2028–2030

The BTO/STO sample-distribution initiative from 2026 removed the material-access bottleneck that had historically delayed oxide MBE adoption: a European photonics developer evaluating BTO as a modulator layer had previously had no commercially available deposition source. With Riber supplying wafer-scale samples, device developers could fabricate and test modulators on their existing lithography infrastructure without committing to a system purchase.

If twenty European and North American research groups and photonics start-ups received samples in 2026, and 15–20 percent converted to ROSIE system inquiries within the 12–18 month commercial validation window, Riber could be fielding three to six additional ROSIE opportunities by late 2027. A 30–50 percent order-conversion rate from that inquiry pool implied one to three incremental system orders in 2028–2030. Against a 5–10 unit per year target by 2030, the seeding programme was not marginal — it was the primary demand-generation mechanism outside the quantum-computing cohort.

## Capital Allocation and Acquisition Optionality

Riber entered 2026 with €7.5 million in cash, no financial debt, and €5.2 million in annualised net income growing at double-digit rates. The Bezons facility appeared adequate for current production volumes and incremental ROSIE builds, given each ROSIE unit represented a bespoke, low-volume, high-ASP assembly rather than a factory-throughput challenge.

A fourth acquisition — following Addon (2004), VG Semicon (2008), and MBE Control Solutions (2015) — remained available. The logical targets were a surface-science MBE specialist extending the research portfolio to 2D materials or wide-bandgap nitrides, or a process-control instrumentation firm whose in-situ metrology could be embedded in the ROSIE workflow, deepening the platform's switching costs. With €7.5 million in cash and a balance sheet capable of supporting €10–15 million of acquisition financing without meaningful leverage, Riber held firepower for a bolt-on in the €5–15 million enterprise-value range — consistent with prior acquisition sizes.

## Valuation Scenarios: What the Market Might Price In

Riber's approximately 384 percent share-price appreciation through May 2026 had already repriced the stock from deep micro-cap obscurity toward multiples implying partial execution of the ROSIE thesis. Against Veeco Instruments (Nasdaq: VECO) — a $600 million-revenue compound-semiconductor and silicon-technology equipment company trading at approximately 2–3× revenue and 20–30× earnings — three scenarios framed the valuation envelope:

| Scenario | Key Assumptions | Revenue 2028E | Net Margin | Earnings | Implied P/E |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bull** | ROSIE 5+ units/yr, licences granted, margins reach 15–16% | €55–60m | 15–16% | €8–9m | 35–40× |
| **Base** | ROSIE 2–3 units/yr, stable MBE 6000, margins 13–14% | €45–50m | 13–14% | €6–7m | 25–30× |
| **Bear** | Licence escalation, ROSIE delayed, margins compress to 10–11% | €38–42m | 10–11% | €4–5m | 15–20× |

Under the bull case, ROSIE's emergence as a recognised silicon-photonics deposition platform would attract re-rating toward multiples the market assigns to high-growth semiconductor capital equipment franchises in category-creation mode. Under the base case, Riber would trade as a quality micro-cap industrial with durable aftermarket revenues and measured ROSIE optionality. Under the bear case, export-control escalation and a ROSIE delay would return the stock toward the depressed multiples that preceded the Geoffroy-era profitability inflection.

What the scenarios shared was an acknowledgement that Riber's investment case in 2026 was no longer a pure MBE narrative. It was a platform transition bet, priced for partial success, with the POEM ecosystem seed programme as the mechanism by which that success either compounded or stalled. The market had begun to notice. Whether the fundamentals would catch the narrative was the question 2027 would begin to answer.
